EndoWAM introduces future grounding, which predicts task-relevant target regions in future observations from intermediate denoising features of a video world model. Specifically, EndoWAM couples a lightweight diffusion transformer for future target-region prediction with a discrete action expert through a shared predictive representation. This design injects target-aware supervision into predictive dynamics modeling, improving robustness to visual degradation and viewpoint changes while enabling real-time control in a single denoising pass. We further introduce EndoMotion, a robotic endoscopic motion dataset spanning three anatomically distinct procedures: ureteroscopy, esophagoscopy, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). EndoWAM consistently outperforms all baselines and alternative grounding strategies, while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to unseen viewpoints, environments, and targets. These results establish EndoWAM as a predictive, target-grounded framework for accurate, generalizable, and long-horizon navigation in visually constrained endoscopic environments.

AI.tldr: EndoWAM introduces the first World Action Model (WAM) for generalizable robotic endoscopic navigation by coupling future grounding (predicting task-relevant target regions in future observations) with action generation through a shared predictive representation. It also introduces EndoMotion, a dataset spanning ureteroscopy, esophagoscopy, and ERCP.
AI.motivation: Autonomous endoscopic navigation reduces clinicians' operational burden but faces robust control challenges due to tissue deformation, transient occlusions, and rapidly changing viewpoints. Existing learning-based policies typically predict actions from current observations without explicitly modeling future dynamics, limiting their robustness and reliability in safety-critical settings.

It couples a lightweight diffusion transformer for future target-region prediction with a discrete action expert through a shared predictive representation. This design injects target-aware supervision into predictive dynamics modeling, enabling real-time control in a single denoising pass.

AI.conclusion: EndoWAM establishes a predictive, target-grounded framework for accurate, generalizable, and long-horizon navigation in visually constrained endoscopic environments, overcoming challenges of limited training data, restricted viewpoint diversity, deformable anatomy, and high inference latency.

title: Hermite Curves as Trajectory Priors for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Project page is available at https://aopolin-lv.github.io/Hermite/
summary: Despite recent progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation, the action chunk remains a weakly structured interface. Existing work typically flatten each chunk into per-timestep controls, relying on implicit data learning that manifests as jagged motion and boundary discontinuities during physical execution. To address these limitations, we introduce Hermite trajectory priors, parameterizing the chunk trajectory as a piecewise cubic Hermite curve defined by endpoint positions and velocities to explicitly enforce smoothness and continuity. We instantiate this fixed operator across discrete autoregressive and continuous generative paradigms via three variants: (1) Hermite Tokens, which predict quantized boundary variables autoregressively; (2) Hermite Scaffold, which decomposes clean actions into a base scaffold and residuals; and (3) Hermite Regularization, which applies the prior strictly as an auxiliary training objective. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot platforms, Hermite Regularization achieves superior performance among these three variants, improving π0.5 baseline success rates from 95.9% to 98.7% on LIBERO, 85.7% to 90.9% on LIBERO-plus, and 63.4% to 90.0% across four real-robot tasks without additional inference overhead. Trajectory analyses reveal that explicitly structuring trajectory priors serves most effectively as a learning inductive bias rather than a runtime constraint.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hermite trajectory priors to improve smoothness in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation by parameterizing action chunks as piecewise cubic Hermite curves.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models flatten action chunks into per-timestep controls, leading to jagged motion and boundary discontinuities due to implicit data learning.
AI.method: Three variants are introduced: (1) Hermite Tokens - autoregressive prediction of quantized boundary variables, (2) Hermite Scaffold - decomposing actions into base scaffold and residuals, (3) Hermite Regularization - applying the prior as an auxiliary training objective.
AI.result: Hermite Regularization achieved superior performance: LIBERO (95.9%→98.7%), LIBERO-plus (85.7%→90.9%), and four real-robot tasks (63.4%→90.0%) without inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly structuring trajectory priors serves most effectively as a learning inductive bias rather than a runtime constraint.

title: DreamTrajectory: Trajectory-Guided Action Generation with World Model Alignment for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to coordinate base and arm motion under continuously changing viewpoints and contact conditions, within an action space far larger than that of fixed-base manipulation. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are limited in two respects. (i)They map observations directly to whole-body action chunks, searching this large action space without an explicit task-space motion plan, which makes coordinated base--arm prediction imprecise. (ii)They execute the predicted chunk open-loop, without checking whether the actions can realize the motion the policy intended, so control errors and unmodeled contacts accumulate into a gap between planned and realized motion. We present DreamTrajectory, a trajectory-guided framework for language-conditioned mobile manipulation that introduces one component for each limitation. Addressing(i), DreamTrajectory jointly predicts an intention-level end-effector trajectory and a whole-body action chunk in a single action expert, so that the trajectory explicitly guides base--arm action generation instead of remaining implicit. Addressing(ii), a lightweight trajectory world model predicts the trajectory that a candidate action chunk would induce, and a test-time search--predict--score procedure selects the candidate best aligned with the planned trajectory. On MS-HAB, trajectory guidance raises average success from 32.3% to 47.5% and test-time refinement further to 54.8%, with the largest gains on contact-rich articulated-object tasks. On three real-world mobile manipulation tasks, the corresponding average success rates are 63.3%, 81.7%, and 90.0%.

title: SG-WAM: Self-Guided World Modeling in Geometry-Aware Policy Space
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) couple action generation with prediction of future states. Their effectiveness depends on whether future dynamics are modeled in a space that is both aligned with action generation and sufficiently geometry-aware to capture where and how actions change the scene. Existing WAMs typically satisfy only part of this requirement, relying on either perceptually heavy observation-space targets or auxiliary latent spaces that are not jointly structured for action relevance and geometry. We propose SG-WAM, a self-guided framework that learns geometry-aware action-conditioned dynamics directly in the policy-derived representation space. SG-WAM introduces learnable dynamics tokens and a Self-Guided World Predictor that forecasts their future latent states conditioned on intervening robot actions. Prediction targets are generated by an exponential moving average copy of the same policy backbone, providing stable supervision within the representation family used by the action expert. Geometric supervision further structures the policy image-token representations, providing spatially grounded context for the dynamics tokens and yielding a future-alignment space that is both action-relevant and geometry-aware. Latent future prediction, geometric grounding, and flow-matching action generation are jointly optimized end-to-end in a unified framework. Built on a 0.9B model without large-scale embodied pretraining, SG-WAM achieves 98.5% average success on LIBERO and 73% on LIBERO-Plus, while outperforming strong baselines in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution real-world evaluations.

AI.tldr: SG-WAM is a self-guided framework that learns geometry-aware action-conditioned dynamics directly in the policy-derived representation space using learnable dynamics tokens and a Self-Guided World Predictor, achieving 98.5% success on LIBERO and 73% on LIBERO-Plus without large-scale embodied pretraining.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) need to balance two requirements: alignment with action generation and geometry-awareness. Existing WAMs only satisfy one of these requirements—either relying on perceptually heavy observation-space targets or auxiliary latent spaces that aren't jointly structured for action relevance and geometry.
AI.method: SG-WAM introduces learnable dynamics tokens and a Self-Guided World Predictor that forecasts future latent states conditioned on robot actions. Prediction targets are generated by an exponential moving average copy of the same policy backbone, providing stable supervision within the representation family. Geometric supervision structures policy image-token representations, and latent future prediction, geometric grounding, and flow-matching action generation are jointly optimized end-to-end.
AI.result: Built on a 0.9B model without large-scale embodied pretraining, SG-WAM achieves 98.5% average success on LIBERO and 73% on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming strong baselines in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution real-world evaluations.
AI.conclusion: SG-WAM demonstrates that a compact model can achieve strong performance in robotic manipulation tasks by learning geometry-aware dynamics directly in the policy space, providing a unified framework for action generation and world modeling that balances action relevance with geometric awareness.

title: Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks and How to Fix Them
summary: We address the problem of understanding when and why Vision-Language-Action models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks that require precise physical interaction. Prior work has primarily focused on addressing contact failures through force-augmented architectures and training-time regularizers, yet the root causes of these failures remain underexplored. We identify two distinct failure modes underlying this gap. Precision failures are rooted in a flow-matching policy training mismatch, and force failures arise from the distinctive structure of force signals. We address each failure mode with a targeted mechanism and combine them into FACT, which achieves 66% average success rate across five contact-rich tasks against 41% for the best prior baseline, in an evaluation spanning almost 2,500 real-world rollouts.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and addresses two failure modes in Vision-Language-Action models for contact-rich manipulation: precision failures (rooted in flow-matching policy training mismatch) and force failures (arising from distinctive force signal structure). The proposed FACT framework combines targeted mechanisms for each failure mode, achieving 66% average success across five tasks vs 41% for the best prior baseline in 2,500 real-world rollouts.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks requiring precise physical interaction. Prior research focused on force-augmented architectures and training-time regularizers but failed to understand the root causes of these failures. A deeper understanding of when and why VLA models fail in contact-rich settings is needed to develop more effective solutions.
AI.method: The authors identify two distinct failure modes: (1) Precision failures, caused by flow-matching policy training mismatch, and (2) Force failures, arising from the distinctive structure of force signals. Each failure mode is addressed with a targeted mechanism, and these are combined into the FACT (Force and Precision) framework to create a unified solution.
AI.result: FACT achieves 66% average success rate across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, compared to 41% for the best prior baseline. The evaluation spans nearly 2,500 real-world rollouts, demonstrating significant performance improvement.
AI.conclusion: By systematically identifying and addressing both precision and force failure modes in contact-rich manipulation, FACT successfully bridges the performance gap between VLA models and human-level performance. The framework demonstrates that understanding and targeting specific failure mechanisms, rather than only architectural modifications, is essential for improving robotic manipulation capabilities.

title: GenTrack: Physical Alignment for Robot-Native Motion Generation and Zero-Shot Humanoid Tracking
summary: General-purpose humanoid trackers can execute diverse references, but their zero-shot coverage depends on large embodied corpora that are costly to extend. Text-to-motion generators offer scalable supervision, yet models trained on human motion or retargeted data inherit a gap between kinematic plausibility and robot executability. Existing one-way pipelines fix either the generated corpus or the reward tracker. We introduce GenTrack, an online generator--tracker framework that alternates execution-grounded, group-relative generator alignment with tracker training on newly generated references; anchoring and rehearsal constrain drift. On Unitree G1, we evaluate GenTrack with ProtoMotions and SONIC backbones across three zero-shot tracking splits including public AMASS and LAFAN benchmarks, and a private out-of-distribution test set of 1,024 prompt-motion pairs in the wild. The online co-training strategy consistently produces generators that output more robot-executable motions with strong semantic alignment, and trackers with markedly broader zero-shot coverage and improved tracking accuracy, especially on out-of-distribution references. These results demonstrate that joint online post-training effectively narrows the executability gap between retargeted references and robot-native motion, advancing zero-shot humanoid control without additional data collection and beyond the limitations of a static reference pool.

AI.tldr: GenTrack is an online generator-tracker framework that co-trains a text-to-motion generator and humanoid tracker on a robot (Unitree G1) to close the gap between kinematic plausibility and robot executability, achieving superior zero-shot tracking performance on public benchmarks and out-of-distribution data without additional data collection.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid trackers require large embodied corpora for zero-shot coverage, while text-to-motion generators lack robot-executability due to the kinematic gap between human motion and robot capabilities. One-way pipelines fix either the corpus or the tracker, leaving the executability gap unresolved and limiting zero-shot control performance.
AI.method: GenTrack implements an online generator-tracker framework that alternates between execution-grounded, group-relative generator alignment and tracker training on newly generated references. The approach uses anchoring and rehearsal mechanisms to constrain drift, co-training on the Unitree G1 robot using ProtoMotions and SONIC backbones.
AI.result: The co-training strategy produces generators that output more robot-executable motions with strong semantic alignment and trackers with markedly broader zero-shot coverage and improved tracking accuracy, particularly on out-of-distribution references. Evaluation across AMASS, LAFAN, and a private OOD test set of 1,024 pairs demonstrates consistent performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Joint online post-training effectively narrows the executability gap between retargeted references and robot-native motion, advancing zero-shot humanoid control without additional data collection and overcoming the limitations of static reference pools.

title: When Replanning Becomes the Bottleneck: Budgeted Replanning for Embodied Agents
comment: 20 pages total: 9 pages main text, 3 pages references, and 8 pages appendix; 18 figures and 32 tables. Accepted at ICML 2026
summary: Embodied agents replan frequently to recover from execution drift, partial observability, and coordination hazards, but each LLM-based replanning call can consume an accumulated textual context that grows over time and across agents. Once this context becomes large, replanning latency develops heavy tails and can miss real-time deadlines even when task success remains high, a failure mode that is hard to detect from average latency or success alone. We present BRACE, a controller that formulates replanning as a budgeted control loop by deciding whether to replan, selecting a replanning mode, and allocating an explicit token budget and latency service-level objective (SLO) while accounting for optional efficiency modules. As a reusable component, we introduce E-RECAP, a cost-aware progressive token pruning method that predicts token utility and prunes replanning contexts across transformer layers while preserving critical head and tail tokens. Across Meta Habitat, RoboFactory, and AirSim, BRACE with E-RECAP reduces replanning-call token counts by 62-92% and SLO violation rates from 85.5-100.0% to 4.7-50.0% in settings where task success is already saturated. In a harder RoboFactory setting where open-loop, frozen-plan, and No BRACE all fail, BRACE + E-RECAP reaches 80.0% success with 4.6% SLO violations, demonstrating that tail-aware per-call budgeting is effective across embodied platforms.

AI.tldr: BRACE is a controller that reduces replanning latency and SLO violations in embodied agents by formulating replanning as a budgeted control loop with token budgeting and progressive token pruning via E-RECAP.
AI.motivation: LLM-based embodied agents replan frequently, but accumulated textual context grows over time, causing heavy-tailed latency and missed real-time deadlines even with high task success. This failure mode is hard to detect from average latency or success metrics alone.
AI.method: BRACE formulates replanning as a budgeted control loop that decides whether to replan, selects a replanning mode, allocates an explicit token budget and latency service-level objective (SLO), and accounts for optional efficiency modules. It introduces E-RECAP, a cost-aware progressive token pruning method that predicts token utility and prunes replanning contexts across transformer layers while preserving critical head and tail tokens.
AI.result: Across Meta Habitat, RoboFactory, and AirSim, BRACE with E-RECAP reduces replanning-call token counts by 62-92% and SLO violation rates from 85.5-100.0% to 4.7-50.0% in settings where task success is already saturated. In a harder RoboFactory setting where baseline methods fail, BRACE + E-RECAP reaches 80.0% success with 4.6% SLO violations.
AI.conclusion: Tail-aware per-call budgeting is effective across embodied platforms for reducing latency and SLO violations while maintaining task success, addressing the heavy-tailed latency problem that traditional metrics fail to capture.

title: DynamicManip: Enabling Dynamic Manipulation from a Single Static Demonstration
summary: Dynamic manipulation is a critical capability for robots operating in complex and dynamic environments, where robots must interact with objects that are moving or require rapid adjustments. However, learning models for dynamic manipulation tasks face two major challenges: (1) the combinatorial complexity of dynamic scenarios leads to substantial data requirements, and (2) rapid variations in dynamics require real-time and accurate policy execution. In this paper, we propose DynamicManip to address these challenges through an efficient data augmentation pipeline and a low-latency imitation policy. We first propose a static-to-dynamic augmentation pipeline that synthesizes diverse dynamic manipulation demonstrations from a single static demonstration. Second, we introduce a dynamic-aware adaptive policy that adjusts its inference frequency according to task dynamics, enabling responsive and effective dynamic manipulation. Third, we build a dynamic manipulation benchmark, which includes diverse dynamic tasks with an automatic evaluation system for scalable and consistent assessment. Extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world demonstrate that DynamicManip not only provides significant improvements in data efficiency but also achieves better performance in dynamic manipulation tasks, with a mean success rate 18.4 percentage points higher and policy-query latency 32.9% lower.

AI.tldr: DynamicManip introduces an efficient data augmentation pipeline and low-latency adaptive policy to enable robots to perform dynamic manipulation tasks with improved data efficiency, higher success rates, and reduced latency.
AI.motivation: Robotic dynamic manipulation in complex environments faces two major challenges: (1) combinatorial complexity leading to substantial data requirements, and (2) rapid variations in dynamics requiring real-time and accurate policy execution.
AI.method: The framework proposes three key contributions: (1) a static-to-dynamic augmentation pipeline that synthesizes diverse dynamic manipulation demonstrations from a single static demonstration, (2) a dynamic-aware adaptive policy that adjusts inference frequency based on task dynamics, and (3) a dynamic manipulation benchmark with diverse tasks and an automatic evaluation system.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate significant improvements: 18.4 percentage points higher mean success rate and 32.9% lower policy-query latency compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: DynamicManip effectively addresses the challenges of data efficiency and real-time execution in dynamic manipulation tasks, achieving superior performance and scalability for robotic systems operating in complex environments.

title: Rapid Embodiment Adaptation for Quadrupedal Locomotion
summary: Humans readily adapt their movements as their bodies change through aging, injury, or load carrying, but learning-based robot policies often break when hardware properties shift. We introduce an online embodiment adaptation framework for quadrupedal locomotion that infers embodiment parameters from short interaction histories and conditions control on the inferred hardware state. Our method pairs a generalist policy trained under embodiment randomization with a lightweight adaptation module that identifies physical changes within half a second. We evaluate two representative forms of embodiment variation: joint-range constraints and trunk-mass changes, corresponding to joint-level kinematic degradation and body-level dynamic variation. In simulation, the module accurately estimates these changes and enables closed-loop control that substantially outperforms policies conditioned directly on interaction history. On a real Unitree Go2 robot, our system maintains stable locomotion under severe instances of the evaluated changes, including a fully locked leg and a 5 kg payload, where non-adaptive methods fail. These results demonstrate the practicality of explicit online embodiment identification for rapid adaptation to joint-limit and payload-mass changes, and provide a step toward handling broader forms of uncertain, degraded, or changing robot hardware.

AI.tldr: An online embodiment adaptation framework for quadrupeds that infers hardware changes from short interaction histories and conditions control policies accordingly, enabling rapid adaptation to joint-limit constraints and payload variations.
AI.motivation: Humans naturally adapt movements to physical changes through aging, injury, or load carrying, but learning-based robot policies fail when hardware properties shift due to joint-range constraints or trunk-mass variations.
AI.method: Pairs a generalist policy trained with embodiment randomization with a lightweight adaptation module that identifies physical changes within 0.5 seconds, inferring embodiment parameters from interaction histories to condition closed-loop control.
AI.result: In simulation, the module accurately estimates changes and substantially outperforms history-conditioned policies. On a real Unitree Go2 robot, the system maintains stable locomotion under severe variations including fully locked legs and 5 kg payloads where non-adaptive methods fail.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the practicality of explicit online embodiment identification for rapid adaptation to joint-limit and payload-mass changes, providing a step toward handling broader forms of uncertain, degraded, or changing robot hardware.

title: Learning Smooth SE(3) Trajectories under Left-Invariant Riemannian Metrics
summary: Optimal trajectory generation for rigid-body motions on Lie groups can be formulated as a variational problem that minimizes energy functionals defined by Riemannian metrics. While closed-form solutions exist for special cases such as product metrics and rest-to-rest boundary conditions, solving the general problem with arbitrary boundary states and coupled rotational-translational metrics often requires computationally expensive numerical boundary value solvers. These limitations restrict the use of geometrically consistent trajectory generation in real-time robotic planning and control. This paper presents a learning-based framework for approximating higher-order smooth trajectories on SE(3) under general left-invariant Riemannian metrics. The method parameterizes body-twist trajectories using high-order polynomials and relies on a neural network to learn a subset of the polynomial coefficients and the trajectory duration. The remaining coefficients are analytically determined to enforce the boundary conditions. The training of the network is guided by losses derived from Euler-Lagrange optimality conditions, metric-weighted smoothness objectives, and feasibility constraints. The metric-conditioned framework enables generalization across diverse metric structures and motion conditions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach generates smooth trajectories that closely approximate solutions from numerical optimization while achieving millisecond-level inference times. We demonstrate two practical applications of the proposed framework: real-time generation of diverse motion primitives with waypoint traversal, and refinement for quadrotor flight under dynamic conditions. These results suggest that learning-based motions with geometric structure can provide an efficient alternative to conventional optimization-based methods for trajectory generation on SE(3).

AI.tldr: A learning-based framework that approximates optimal SE(3) trajectories with millisecond-level inference by parameterizing body-twist trajectories with polynomials and a neural network, trained on Euler-Lagrange optimality conditions and feasibility constraints.
AI.motivation: Closed-form solutions for optimal trajectory generation on SE(3) only exist for special cases (product metrics, rest-to-rest boundary conditions). General problems with arbitrary boundary states and coupled rotational-translational metrics require computationally expensive numerical boundary value solvers, restricting real-time robotic planning and control applications.
AI.method: The method parameterizes body-twist trajectories using high-order polynomials, where a neural network learns a subset of polynomial coefficients and trajectory duration while remaining coefficients are analytically determined to enforce boundary conditions. Training losses incorporate Euler-Lagrange optimality conditions, metric-weighted smoothness objectives, and feasibility constraints. The framework is metric-conditioned to enable generalization across diverse metric structures.
AI.result: The approach generates smooth trajectories that closely approximate numerical optimization solutions while achieving millisecond-level inference times. Two practical applications demonstrated: real-time generation of diverse motion primitives with waypoint traversal, and quadrotor flight refinement under dynamic conditions.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based motions with geometric structure provide an efficient alternative to conventional optimization-based methods for SE(3) trajectory generation, enabling real-time applications that were previously limited by expensive numerical solvers.

title: Uncovering and Mitigating Positional Blind Spots in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve promising performance in robotic manipulation, typically measured by success rates aggregated over predefined object configurations, an evaluation that implicitly assumes spatially uniform competence across the workspace. However, this assumption does not hold: even with the instruction and every other scene factor held fixed, merely relocating a task-irrelevant distractor can sharply raise the failure probability within localized, spatially coherent regions, which we term Positional Blind Spots (PBS). In this paper, we propose a two-stage black-box framework to uncover and mitigate PBS. During the uncovering stage, we grid the workspace and apply a one-sided log-likelihood-ratio test to localize PBS cells with significantly elevated risk. During the mitigation stage, we fine-tune the policy via LoRA on demonstrations collected from these PBS regions, improving competence there while largely preserving performance across the rest of the workspace. We evaluate our framework on five state-of-the-art VLA policies across two benchmarks, and find that PBS are pervasive and spatially concentrated in all of them, with failure rates up to 0.58. Our search strategy achieves an average F1-score of 0.678, outperforming random search and adaptive sampling baselines by 0.268 and 0.178, respectively. Guided by the discovered regions, targeted fine-tuning reduces the overall failure rate by 40.00%--85.19%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage framework to discover and mitigate Positional Blind Spots (PBS) in Vision-Language-Action models—localized regions where failure rates spike due to task-irrelevant distractors. Using a one-sided log-likelihood-ratio test on a grid, PBS are identified, then targeted fine-tuning via LoRA on demonstrations from these regions reduces overall failure rates by 40-85%.
AI.motivation: VLA models are typically evaluated assuming spatially uniform competence across the workspace, but this assumption is invalid. Even with fixed instructions and scenes, merely relocating task-irrelevant distractors can cause sharp increases in failure probability in localized spatial regions, which the authors term Positional Blind Spots (PBS).
AI.method: A two-stage black-box framework: (1) Uncovering stage—grid the workspace and apply a one-sided log-likelihood-ratio test to localize PBS cells with significantly elevated risk; (2) Mitigation stage—fine-tune the policy via LoRA on demonstrations collected from the discovered PBS regions.
AI.result: PBS are pervasive and spatially concentrated across five SOTA VLA policies on two benchmarks, with failure rates up to 0.58. The search strategy achieves an average F1-score of 0.678, outperforming random search and adaptive sampling by 0.268 and 0.178 respectively. Guided fine-tuning reduces overall failure rates by 40.00%-85.19%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully uncovers and mitigates PBS, improving competence in problematic spatial regions while largely preserving performance across the rest of the workspace. PBS are a significant issue in VLA policies that requires targeted intervention.

title: Perception-and-action system for humanoid robot task execution in construction
summary: Humanoid robots, with their human-like shape and multi-tasking capabilities, are well-aligned with human-dominated workplaces, like those in civil and construction engineering, where they could collaborate with human workers or autonomously perform physically demanding and hazardous tasks. Despite this promise, limited research has explored how to endow these robots with the practical capabilities needed to perform construction tasks. To this end, this study proposes a novel perception-and-action system that enables humanoid robots to learn and perform construction tasks from worker demonstrations. This system contains two deep networks: Humanoid-PoseNet, which extracts human postures and translates them into mechanically feasible poses for a humanoid robot; and Humanoid-ActionNet, which learns robot-executable actions based on these translated poses. Experimental results demonstrate that the humanoid robot reliably executed eight construction-related actions, achieving an average motion-tracking error of 82.45 mm MPJPE (Mean Per Joint Position Error). This work provides an early step toward deploying humanoid collaborators in construction.

AI.tldr: A novel perception-and-action system enabling humanoid robots to learn construction tasks from human demonstrations using Humanoid-PoseNet and Humanoid-ActionNet deep networks, achieving an average motion-tracking error of 82.45 mm MPJPE across eight construction actions.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots are well-suited for human-dominated workplaces like civil and construction engineering, but limited research exists on endowing them with practical capabilities to perform construction tasks, creating a gap for deploying collaborative humanoid robots in this domain.
AI.method: The proposed system comprises two deep networks: 1) Humanoid-PoseNet, which extracts human postures and translates them into mechanically feasible poses for a humanoid robot; 2) Humanoid-ActionNet, which learns robot-executable actions based on the translated poses. This architecture enables robots to learn construction tasks from worker demonstrations.
AI.result: The humanoid robot reliably executed eight construction-related actions with an average motion-tracking error of 82.45 mm MPJPE (Mean Per Joint Position Error), demonstrating successful task execution from demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: This research provides an early step toward deploying humanoid collaborators in construction, addressing the gap in practical capabilities for construction tasks and representing a significant advancement toward human-robot collaboration in civil and construction engineering environments.

title: AffordTrajDP: Dynamic Affordance-Guided Visuomotor Policy Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Affordance-guided imitation learning has shown impressive performance in robotic manipulation tasks by compressing visual perception into task-specific geometric constraints (e.g., fixed contact points). However, the commonly used static affordances can become inconsistent in precision-critical tasks or under object location perturbations, leading to post-contact trajectory drift. To address this issue, we propose AffordTrajDP, a dynamic framework that constructs affordance trajectories via object-centric temporal propagation to guide the progressive manipulation process. Specifically, given an RGB-D observation, our core insight is that a retrieved anchor affordance, which captures the desired contact point between the end-effector and the target object, can be propagated forward via affordance propagation, using the object's SE(3) pose as a natural propagation medium, to yield an affordance trajectory that provides temporally consistent, state-aware guidance throughout execution. AffordTrajDP achieves 70.0% average success rate on ManiSkill3, outperforming strong baselines by up to 17.8%. Real-world experiments on Galaxea A1 and UR7e robotic arms, covering StackCube, PickCup, AdapterInsertion, Ring-on-Peg, Put-in-Bowl, and USB Insertion, further validate robustness under object placement variations and appearance changes, with seen and unseen object instances evaluated on Galaxea A1, and ablations confirm the contribution of each proposed component.

AI.tldr: AffordTrajDP is a dynamic framework that constructs affordance trajectories via object-centric temporal propagation to provide temporally consistent guidance for robotic manipulation, achieving 70% success rate on ManiSkill3 and validated on real-world robotic arms.
AI.motivation: Static affordances in affordance-guided imitation learning become inconsistent under object location perturbations or in precision-critical tasks, leading to post-contact trajectory drift that degrades manipulation performance.
AI.method: Given an RGB-D observation, AffordTrajDP retrieves an anchor affordance representing the desired contact point and propagates it forward using the object's SE(3) pose as a natural propagation medium, constructing an affordance trajectory that provides temporally consistent, state-aware guidance throughout execution.
AI.result: Achieves 70.0% average success rate on ManiSkill3, outperforming strong baselines by up to 17.8%; real-world experiments on Galaxea A1 and UR7e arms across 6 tasks (StackCube, PickCup, AdapterInsertion, Ring-on-Peg, Put-in-Bowl, USB Insertion) demonstrate robustness under object placement variations and appearance changes, including unseen object instances.
AI.conclusion: The object-centric temporal propagation approach effectively addresses post-contact trajectory drift by maintaining temporal consistency, and validation across multiple robotic platforms and object variations confirms the framework's effectiveness for precision-critical robotic manipulation tasks.

title: A Forward-Inverse Dynamic Game Framework for Enhanced Multi-Agent Trajectory Planning
summary: This paper studies feedback Nash equilibrium (FBNE) seeking for multi-agent trajectory planning in nonlinear dynamical systems with unknown agents' objectives and state-dependent inter-agent coupling. While dynamic game theory provides a principled framework for such problems, existing approaches typically assume fully rational agents with known objectives or rely on fixed regularization, limiting their ability to capture bounded rationality and spatially varying interaction intensity in safety-critical settings. To this end, we propose a KL-regularized dynamic game with a state-dependent weight that adaptively balances optimality and behavioral priors. To infer unknown cost parameters from demonstrated behaviors, we develop a context-aware inverse game module based on maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning with physics-informed regularization, ensuring structural consistency with the forward game. We establish per-iteration well-posedness of the regularized local game and show that the adaptive weighting function remains Lipschitz continuous under bounded nominal-trajectory updates. Numerical simulations and multi-robot experiments on cooperative navigation and merging scenarios validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: A KL-regularized dynamic game framework with adaptive state-dependent weighting and context-aware inverse reinforcement learning for multi-agent trajectory planning in safety-critical systems with unknown objectives and inter-agent coupling.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic game approaches for multi-agent trajectory planning assume fully rational agents with known objectives or fixed regularization, limiting their ability to capture bounded rationality and spatially varying interaction intensity in safety-critical settings.
AI.method: A KL-regularized dynamic game with state-dependent weight adaptively balancing optimality and behavioral priors, combined with a context-aware inverse game module based on maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning with physics-informed regularization to infer unknown cost parameters from demonstrated behaviors. The approach establishes per-iteration well-posedness of the regularized local game and shows the adaptive weighting function remains Lipschitz continuous under bounded nominal-trajectory updates.
AI.result: Numerical simulations and multi-robot experiments on cooperative navigation and merging scenarios validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables robust multi-agent trajectory planning in safety-critical settings by effectively balancing optimality and behavioral priors while handling unknown agent objectives and state-dependent inter-agent coupling.

title: SyncPlan: Long-Horizon LLM Coordination with Explicit Synchronization and Adaptive Correction
summary: LLM-based multi-agent coordination faces a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and adaptivity in dynamic environments. Existing approaches typically rely on repeated LLM invocations or multi-round communication to adapt decisions during execution, introducing substantial latency and making coordination vulnerable to asynchronous progress and environmental changes. Conversely, one-shot planning reduces coordination overhead but produces open-loop plans that can quickly become stale or fail when actions depend on other agents and the environment. We introduce SyncPlan, a plan-execute-correct framework for long-horizon coordination through explicit synchronization and adaptive correction. Given the state and team-level task, a centralized LLM coordinator generates per-agent action chains in a single planning call. During execution, explicit wait primitives and deadlock detection enforce inter-agent and agent-environment dependencies, while a lightweight Plan Staleness Detector continuously assesses the remaining plan and triggers replanning when environmental changes invalidate its assumptions. We further optimize the coordinator through SFT and planning-oriented RL with dense task progress and outcome-level execution feedback. Experiments on the public Overcooked benchmark and the complex Honor of Kings environment show that SyncPlan achieves state-of-the-art task success rates while using less than 0.05% of the wall-clock runtime compared with existing LLM-based coordinators. Code and datasets will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: SyncPlan is a plan-execute-correct framework for LLM-based multi-agent coordination that balances efficiency and adaptivity through explicit synchronization, deadlock detection, and adaptive replanning triggered by plan staleness detection.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent coordination faces a fundamental trade-off: existing approaches either use repeated LLM invocations (high latency, vulnerable to async progress) or one-shot planning (open-loop, quickly stale). A unified approach addressing both efficiency and adaptivity is needed.
AI.method: SyncPlan introduces: 1) A centralized LLM coordinator generating per-agent action chains in a single planning call; 2) Explicit wait primitives and deadlock detection for inter-agent/environment dependencies; 3) A lightweight Plan Staleness Detector that triggers adaptive replanning; 4) SFT and planning-oriented RL with dense feedback to optimize the coordinator.
AI.result: On Overcooked and Honor of Kings benchmarks, SyncPlan achieves state-of-the-art task success rates while using less than 0.05% of the wall-clock runtime compared to existing LLM-based coordinators.
AI.conclusion: SyncPlan effectively balances efficiency and adaptivity in dynamic multi-agent coordination scenarios, delivering superior performance with minimal computational overhead through explicit synchronization and adaptive correction mechanisms.

title: ProtoAct: Turning Wet-Lab Protocols into Embodied Robotic Actions
summary: Biological wet-lab protocols are written for trained researchers and often leave routine operations, state-dependent conditions, and contextual parameters implicit, making them difficult to translate into robot-executable actions. We present ProtoAct, a structured protocol-grounding framework that converts free-form biological procedures into state-aware, embodiment-ready action sequences. ProtoAct uses ProtoRAG to retrieve manually annotated examples for context-sensitive parsing, employs RefineChecker to detect and revise missing or inconsistent steps, and applies ActSchema to map the refined procedure into constrained JSON function sequences. We further introduce BioP2E, for which we manually annotate 22 cell-culture protocols into 258 monitoring conditions, 910 executable subtasks, and 962 grounded action calls. Evaluation across seven large language models demonstrates that ProtoAct can be effectively instantiated with different backbones. Ablations confirm that retrieval, posterior checking, and schema constraints make complementary contributions. The parsed subtasks further support demonstration collection and VLA model training, enabling successful execution in both simulation and real-robot settings. ProtoAct thus provides a practical interface between biological protocol understanding and embodied robotic execution.

AI.tldr: ProtoAct is a framework that converts free-form biological protocols into state-aware, robot-executable action sequences through retrieval-augmented parsing, step refinement, and schema mapping, with a BioP2E dataset of 22 cell-culture protocols annotated into 258 monitoring conditions, 910 subtasks, and 962 grounded actions.
AI.motivation: Biological wet-lab protocols are written for human researchers and implicitly contain routine operations, state-dependent conditions, and contextual parameters, making them difficult to translate directly into robot-executable actions without explicit grounding.
AI.method: ProtoAct employs three core components: (1) ProtoRAG for retrieving manually annotated examples to enable context-sensitive parsing, (2) RefineChecker for detecting and revising missing or inconsistent steps, and (3) ActSchema for mapping refined procedures into constrained JSON function sequences. The system is evaluated across 7 LLM backbones.
AI.result: ProtoAct demonstrates effective instantiation with different LLM backbones. Ablation studies confirm that retrieval, posterior checking, and schema constraints provide complementary contributions. The parsed subtasks successfully support demonstration collection and VLA model training, enabling execution in both simulation and real-robot environments.
AI.conclusion: ProtoAct provides a practical interface bridging biological protocol understanding and embodied robotic execution, enabling automated translation of human-readable protocols into machine-executable action sequences for laboratory automation.

title: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap in Parallel-Link Leg Mechanisms via Simulator-Side Dynamics Normalization
summary: This paper addresses the sim-to-real gap in dynamics arising when a parallel-link mechanism is represented by a serial-tree surrogate in simulation. Conventional Jacobian-based state and torque mappings preserve consistency with the kinematic and virtual-work relations but do not account for the coordinate-induced redistribution of actuator inertia and damping and the linkage inertia omitted during serial-tree reduction. To address this gap, Simulator-Side System Normalization (S3N) is proposed to normalize the serial-tree simulator's effective dynamics while preserving its tree topology. S3N-Act incorporates actuator inertia and damping into the serial-coordinate dynamics through coordinate transformation, whereas S3N-Full restores residual linkage inertia by separately identifying actuator- and leg-level frequency responses. In the 2-DoF validation, S3N-Full reduced the joint-position and torque RMSEs by 80.9% and 82.1%, respectively, relative to the Jacobian-mapping baseline. During pitch-in-place motion, S3N-Act and S3N-Full reduced the RMSE of the ground reaction force norm by 65.1% and 62.4%, respectively. During circular locomotion, S3N-Full reduced the phase-averaged, command-normalized sim-to-real gap from 17.3% to 9.9%. These results show that simulator-side normalization improves motion- and force-level sim-to-real consistency. It enables policy training in a serial-tree framework with hardware-consistent dynamics that better represent the physical parallel-link mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Simulator-Side System Normalization (S3N) to address the sim-to-real gap in parallel-link mechanisms represented by serial-tree surrogates, improving dynamics consistency through coordinate transformation and residual inertia restoration.
AI.motivation: Conventional Jacobian-based state and torque mappings preserve kinematic consistency but fail to account for coordinate-induced redistribution of actuator inertia/damping and omitted linkage inertia during serial-tree reduction, leading to significant sim-to-real gaps.
AI.method: Two variants of Simulator-Side System Normalization (S3N): (1) S3N-Act incorporates actuator inertia and damping through coordinate transformation, and (2) S3N-Full restores residual linkage inertia by separately identifying actuator- and leg-level frequency responses while preserving tree topology.
AI.result: S3N-Full reduced 2-DoF joint-position and torque RMSEs by 80.9% and 82.1% respectively; reduced ground reaction force norm RMSE by 65.1% (S3N-Act) and 62.4% (S3N-Full) during pitch-in-place motion; reduced phase-averaged, command-normalized sim-to-real gap from 17.3% to 9.9% during circular locomotion.
AI.conclusion: Simulator-side normalization significantly improves motion- and force-level sim-to-real consistency, enabling policy training in a serial-tree framework with hardware-consistent dynamics that better represent physical parallel-link mechanisms.

title: TWINS: A Tactile Wearable Isomorphic Arm Networked System for Contact-Rich Manipulation Learning
summary: Recent advances in robot learning for manipulation have increased the importance of collecting real-world demonstration data. However, existing robotic systems primarily focus on end-effector manipulation, making it difficult to teach and execute manipulation tasks involving body-surface contact with the arms and chest. This paper presents TWINS (Tactile Wearable Isomorphic Arm Networked System), a robotic system for manipulation involving body-surface contact. TWINS consists of a Wearable Dual-Arm Device, which is worn by the operator, and an Isomorphic Robot with the same joint configuration and external dimensions. Distributed tactile sensors embedded in the chest and arms enable the measurement of body-surface contact synchronized with joint motion. Using the Wearable Dual-Arm Device, we collected demonstrations for four manipulation tasks involving body-surface contact. We then trained imitation learning policies using the collected demonstrations and deployed them on the Isomorphic Robot, enabling manipulation guided by body-surface tactile observations. Experimental results demonstrate that TWINS provides a unified robotic system for demonstration, learning, and execution of manipulation involving body-surface contact. https://mmurooka.github.io/twins-project-page/

AI.tldr: TWINS is a robotic system for manipulation involving body-surface contact that uses a wearable dual-arm device and an isomorphic robot with distributed tactile sensors on the chest and arms to collect demonstrations and train imitation learning policies.
AI.motivation: Recent advances in robot learning for manipulation have increased the importance of collecting real-world demonstration data, but existing robotic systems primarily focus on end-effector manipulation, making it difficult to teach and execute manipulation tasks involving body-surface contact with the arms and chest.
AI.method: TWINS consists of a Wearable Dual-Arm Device worn by the operator and an Isomorphic Robot with the same joint configuration and external dimensions. Distributed tactile sensors embedded in the chest and arms enable measurement of body-surface contact synchronized with joint motion. The system collected demonstrations for four manipulation tasks and trained imitation learning policies using these demonstrations.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that TWINS successfully enables manipulation guided by body-surface tactile observations, providing a unified robotic system for demonstration, learning, and execution of manipulation involving body-surface contact.
AI.conclusion: TWINS effectively addresses the challenge of manipulation tasks involving body-surface contact by combining wearable sensing with isomorphic robotics, demonstrating that imitation learning policies trained from body-surface tactile demonstrations can be successfully deployed on the isomorphic robot for manipulation tasks.

title: A Tilt-Rotor UAV with a Gripper for Stable Contact-Based Tasks via Environmental Anchoring

summary: Maintaining a stable pose during physical interaction is a significant challenge for aerial robots, often limiting their use in contact-based tasks. This paper presents a novel uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) platform designed to transition from unconstrained flight to a stable, constrained work platform via environmental anchoring. Our system comprises: 1) a multirotor with a tilt-rotor mechanism that decouples pitch from forward motion, enabling stable hover at non-zero pitch angles, and 2) a novel underactuated, cable-driven, prismatic gripper featuring compliance to adapt to irregular geometries, designed to stabilize the UAV by anchoring it to its environment. We present the design and prototyping of the complete system and validate its performance through a series of real-robot flight tests. Results demonstrate that anchoring significantly improves stability for interaction tasks, reducing positional drift RMSE by over 95% compared to a free-flight baseline, even under windy conditions. The anchored system can withstand longitudinal reaction forces up to 75N while maintaining a stable pose. Furthermore, across a range of target geometries and orientations, the system demonstrated consistent stability with a positional drift RMSE that never exceeded 3mm. These results establish the viability of our approach for complex physical interaction tasks, such as sampling tree health by drilling or sensor installation in hard-to-reach locations. AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel UAV platform that transitions from unconstrained flight to a stable, constrained work platform via environmental anchoring using a tilt-rotor mechanism and a cable-driven prismatic gripper with compliance.
AI.motivation: Maintaining a stable pose during physical interaction is a significant challenge for aerial robots, which limits their use in contact-based tasks.
AI.method: The system comprises: 1) a multirotor with a tilt-rotor mechanism that decouples pitch from forward motion, enabling stable hover at non-zero pitch angles, and 2) a novel underactuated, cable-driven, prismatic gripper featuring compliance to adapt to irregular geometries, designed to stabilize the UAV by anchoring it to its environment.
AI.result: Anchoring significantly improves stability, reducing positional drift RMSE by over 95% compared to free-flight baseline, with the system withstanding longitudinal reaction forces up to 75N and maintaining positional drift RMSE never exceeding 3mm across various target geometries and orientations.
AI.conclusion: The results establish the viability of the anchored approach for complex physical interaction tasks, such as sampling tree health by drilling or sensor installation in hard-to-reach locations.

title: Hybrid Impedance-Admittance Control with Multi-Link Aerial Robot for Contact-Rich Surface Sliding Task
summary: Multi-link aerial robots can actively deform their articulated structures during flight, giving them strong potential for aerial manipulation. However, they still face substantial challenges in contact-rich aerial manipulation tasks such as surface sliding, which requires both disturbance robustness and compliance to uncertain surface geometry. Force-control strategies such as impedance and admittance control are commonly employed to address these requirements. Although impedance control can provide disturbance-resistant interaction and admittance control can offer compliant adaptation, their opposite force--motion causalities prevent their simultaneous implementation when applied through the same actuation source, such as the rotor thrusts used by conventional aerial robots. To overcome this limitation, we propose a hybrid impedance--admittance control strategy for a multi-link aerial robot. The articulated morphology enables a functional separation of force and motion regulation across joint and rotor actuation sources. In this framework, admittance behavior is generated through joint angle regulation to enhance adaptive interaction, while impedance behavior is achieved by modulating rotor thrust to regulate the sliding motion. This structural coordination allows the robot to leverage the complementary strengths of both control paradigms. As a result, the multi-link aerial robot achieves resilient and adaptive surface sliding. Experimental results demonstrate robust and compliant sliding performance on unknown surfaces.

AI.tldr: A hybrid impedance-admittance control strategy for multi-link aerial robots enables resilient and adaptive surface sliding on unknown surfaces by decoupling force and motion regulation across joint and rotor actuation.
AI.motivation: Multi-link aerial robots have strong potential for aerial manipulation but face challenges in contact-rich tasks like surface sliding, which require both disturbance robustness and compliance to uncertain surface geometry. Traditional impedance and admittance controls have opposite force-motion causalities that prevent their simultaneous implementation through the same actuation source like rotor thrusts.
AI.method: The paper proposes a hybrid impedance-admittance control strategy that leverages the articulated morphology of multi-link aerial robots to achieve functional separation of force and motion regulation. Admittance behavior is generated through joint angle regulation for adaptive interaction, while impedance behavior is achieved by modulating rotor thrust to regulate sliding motion.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the multi-link aerial robot achieves robust and compliant sliding performance on unknown surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The proposed structural coordination enables simultaneous utilization of complementary strengths from both impedance and admittance control paradigms, overcoming their opposite force-motion causalities and enabling resilient and adaptive surface sliding.

title: ReTouch: Empowering Contact-Rich Dexterous Manipulation with Online-Refined Tactile Prediction
summary: Fusing tactile signals has proven effective for contact-rich manipulation, enabling robots to perceive contact states and adapt to rapidly changing physical interactions. Yet effectively integrating tactile feedback into dexterous manipulation remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce ReTouch, a vision-language-action model (VLA) that supports contact-rich dexterous manipulation through tactile predictions continually refined online using execution-time feedback. ReTouch builds on two main innovations for tactile representation and closed-loop action generation. First, its Tactile-Patch Encoder represents tactile observations as structured tactile patch features that preserve finger identity and local contact structure, providing contact cues for fine-grained dexterous control. Second, its high-frequency action module jointly predicts future tactile states and action chunks and refines both using incoming tactile feedback during execution. This closed-loop refinement keeps tactile predictions aligned with evolving physical interactions, enabling responsive action correction and improving robustness to contact changes and execution errors. We further introduce XHT-Dataset, comprising 900 real-world demonstrations across seven contact-rich tasks collected on an XHand--UR7e platform, and evaluate ReTouch through closed-loop real-robot experiments. ReTouch surpasses the strongest baseline by 18.4 and 23.8 percentage points in average success rate under standard and challenging conditions, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

AI.tldr: ReTouch is a vision-language-action model for contact-rich dexterous manipulation that refines tactile predictions online using execution-time feedback, achieving 18.4% and 23.8% higher success rates than baselines under standard and challenging conditions respectively.
AI.motivation: While tactile signals are effective for contact-rich manipulation, effectively integrating tactile feedback into dexterous manipulation remains underexplored. The challenge lies in creating models that can perceive contact states and adapt to rapidly changing physical interactions during manipulation tasks.
AI.method: ReTouch introduces two key innovations: (1) Tactile-Patch Encoder that represents tactile observations as structured patch features preserving finger identity and local contact structure, and (2) a high-frequency action module that jointly predicts future tactile states and action chunks while refining both using incoming tactile feedback during execution. The model also uses XHT-Dataset containing 900 real-world demonstrations across seven contact-rich tasks on an XHand-UR7e platform.
AI.result: ReTouch surpasses the strongest baseline by 18.4 percentage points in average success rate under standard conditions and 23.8 percentage points under challenging conditions in closed-loop real-robot experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop refinement mechanism keeps tactile predictions aligned with evolving physical interactions, enabling responsive action correction and improving robustness to contact changes and execution errors, suggesting that continuous tactile feedback integration is crucial for high-performance dexterous manipulation.

title: Multi-View Unified Camera Fields: Geometry-Shaped Action-Facing Representations for RGB-Only Multi-Camera VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet complex contact-rich tasks often benefit from multi-camera observations that jointly capture the end effector, objects, and targets under occlusion. Existing multi-camera VLAs usually concatenate view tokens, leaving action representations weak in metric depth and inconsistent across cameras. We introduce Multi-View Unified Camera Fields (MVUCF), a training-only framework that forms a shared action-facing latent field across views. A coordinate-query depth objective makes metric depth recoverable, while a preprocessing-aware correspondence objective aligns tokens observing the same physical point from different cameras. Both directly shape the hidden states consumed by the action module. After geometry injection, depth, camera calibration, and auxiliary heads are removed, so deployment uses the original RGB-only graph with no extra inference FLOPs. Held-out probes confirm stronger depth recovery and cross-view matching. Under matched GR00T-N1.6 settings, MVUCF reaches 98.9% on LIBERO, improves LIBERO-Plus by 22.4 points, and raises success by 23.3 points across six RoboTwin tasks spanning three action families: touch, move-and-place, and contact interaction. Real-world humanoid experiments further provide evidence of its practical effectiveness under RGB-only deployment.

AI.tldr: MVUCF is a training-only framework that creates a shared action-facing latent field across multiple camera views in Vision-Language-Action models. It uses a coordinate-query depth objective to recover metric depth and a preprocessing-aware correspondence objective to align tokens from different cameras observing the same physical point. After geometry injection, the model can be deployed with RGB-only input without additional inference FLOPs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin tasks.
AI.motivation: Complex contact-rich robotic tasks require multi-camera observations to capture end effectors, objects, and targets under occlusion. Existing multi-camera VLA models concatenate view tokens, resulting in weak metric depth representations and inconsistent action representations across cameras.
AI.method: MVUCF introduces two key training objectives: 1) Coordinate-query depth objective that makes metric depth recoverable from the latent field, and 2) Preprocessing-aware correspondence objective that aligns tokens observing the same physical point from different cameras. These objectives shape the hidden states consumed by the action module. The framework forms a shared action-facing latent field across views, and after geometry injection, depth, camera calibration, and auxiliary heads are removed for deployment.
AI.result: MVUCF achieves 98.9% success on LIBERO, improves LIBERO-Plus by 22.4 points, and raises success by 23.3 points across six RoboTwin tasks spanning touch, move-and-place, and contact interaction action families. Held-out probes confirm stronger depth recovery and cross-view matching. Real-world humanoid experiments demonstrate practical effectiveness under RGB-only deployment with no extra inference FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: MVUCF effectively addresses the limitations of existing multi-camera VLA models by creating a unified action-facing latent field that provides consistent, metric-depth-aware representations across multiple views. The training-only approach allows deployment with RGB-only input, making it practical for real-world robotic applications. The significant performance improvements across diverse task families and real-world validation demonstrate its effectiveness for complex contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: Teleopit: A Full-Embodiment Humanoid Teleoperation System
summary: Humanoid teleoperation for demonstration collection requires coordinated whole-body motion, continuous dexterous hand control, and viewpoint control. Existing systems either simplify hand commands or depend on dedicated wearable sensors for fine-grained hand motion. We introduce Teleopit, a full-embodiment teleoperation system that maps body, hand, and head signals from VR to a humanoid body, configurable dexterous hands, and a 2-DoF active vision module. A history encoder and failure-aware rewind sampling improve the motion tracker on both motion-capture and live VR references. An optimization-based hand retargeter combines normalized finger directions, fingertip closure, and thumb-frame alignment to map human hand motion to different dexterous hands without tuning hand-specific objective or solver hyperparameters. Component experiments evaluate tracking success rate and retargeting behavior, while real-robot teleoperation demonstrates coordinated locomotion, manipulation, and viewpoint control. ACT and GR00T N1.7 policies trained on 96 successful demonstrations collected with Teleopit achieve task success rates of 90.0% and 95.0%, respectively, when deployed on the humanoid. The project page is available at https://botrunner64.github.io/teleopit-page.

AI.tldr: Teleopit is a full-embodiment VR teleoperation system mapping body, hand, and head signals to humanoid robots with configurable dexterous hands and active vision, achieving 90-95% task success rates in demonstration collection.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid teleoperation systems have limitations: they either simplify hand commands or depend on dedicated wearable sensors for fine-grained hand motion. There is a need for systems that provide coordinated whole-body motion, continuous dexterous hand control, and viewpoint control simultaneously.
AI.method: Teleopit maps VR body, hand, and head signals to a humanoid body with configurable dexterous hands and a 2-DoF active vision module. It uses a history encoder and failure-aware rewind sampling to improve motion tracking. An optimization-based hand retargeter combines normalized finger directions, fingertip closure, and thumb-frame alignment to map human hand motion to different dexterous hands without requiring hand-specific tuning.
AI.result: Component experiments show improved tracking success rate and retargeting behavior. Real-robot teleoperation demonstrates coordinated locomotion, manipulation, and viewpoint control. Policies trained on 96 Teleopit demonstrations achieve 90.0% (ACT) and 95.0% (GR00T N1.7) task success rates when deployed on the humanoid.
AI.conclusion: Teleopit enables effective full-embodiment teleoperation for demonstration collection, achieving high task success rates without requiring hand-specific tuning or dedicated wearable sensors for fine-grained hand control.

title: Weights or Skills? A Survey of Robot-Learning Techniques: from Action-Predicting Weights to Robots that Write their Own Skills
summary: Robot learning is splitting into two bets: policies that bake competence into frozen weights (vision-language-action, or VLA, models), and agents that write and refine their own executable skills as code. This survey organises the field around that axis of weights versus skills. Its central analytical contribution is a deep-dive that arranges code-as-policy methods by their degree of self-improvement, from zero-shot program synthesis, through closed-loop self-repair and persistent skill memory, to the sparsely populated cell in which execution feedback, skill memory, and evolutionary search combine into one open-ended loop; only a few very recent systems (for example ASPIRE, ENPIRE, and RoboClaw) occupy that cell. We map the complementary "skills" pole, from unsupervised reinforcement-learning skill discovery to large-language-model skill libraries, and show that the word "skill" is used in at least five distinct senses, of which only the code sense self-improves without gradient updates. We then connect the taxonomy to the emerging skill economy: commercial robot-skill marketplaces now distribute one-tap skills across robots but ship only static playback, which surfaces open problems of adaptation, cross-embodiment portability, provenance, safety verification, composition, and standardisation. This is a deliberately focused survey. Rather than cataloguing the field exhaustively, it examines 77 representative systems across six technique families through one taxonomy and a set of contrast tables, and it supplies operational definitions of the self-improvement mechanisms together with a statement of what each family cannot do.

AI.tldr: This survey organizes robot learning methods along two axes: frozen-weight policies (VLA models) vs. agents that write/refine executable skills as code. It categorizes code-as-policy methods by degree of self-improvement and connects this taxonomy to the emerging skill economy.
AI.motivation: Robot learning is splitting into two approaches: policies with frozen weights (VLA models) and agents that write/refine their own skills as code. A systematic organization of this emerging landscape is needed.
AI.method: Organizes the field around the weights vs. skills axis, conducts deep-dive into code-as-policy methods arranged by self-improvement degree, examines 77 representative systems across six technique families, maps the "skills" pole, and connects taxonomy to the skill economy. Provides operational definitions of self-improvement mechanisms.
AI.result: Identifies "skill" used in at least five distinct senses, with only the code sense self-improving without gradient updates. Maps emerging skill economy and identifies open problems: adaptation, cross-embodiment portability, provenance, safety verification, composition, and standardization. Only ASPIRE, ENPIRE, and RoboClaw occupy the cell combining execution feedback, skill memory, and evolutionary search.
AI.conclusion: A focused survey providing operational definitions of self-improvement mechanisms and identifying limitations of each technique family, rather than exhaustive cataloguing.

title: RADAR Perception for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance onboard small-scale Quadrotor UAVs
comment: This work has been submitted for publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice
summary: Fast dynamic obstacle avoidance (DOA) on uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) demands not only low-latency control and actuation but also reliable perception with sufficient sensing range for accurate obstacle detection and speed estimation. This letter presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first mmWave RADAR-based perception-and-control system for fast onboard DOA. We derive and analyze latency and spatial bounds that relate sensing range, relative speed, and control delay, yielding sufficient conditions for successful avoidance. Our system adopts a lightweight tracker based on interacting multiple models and a controller based on control-barrier functions that directly outputs evasive accelerations. It achieves position errors of less than 0.15 m, 0.93 m, and 0.87 m in x, y, and z directions for 300 experiments with three different object sizes and varying visibility (light and dark), and a similar spread for 90 experiments in smoke. An onboard implementation on a Raspberry Pi 4B demonstrates real-time feasibility with an end-to-end sensing-to-command latency of approximately 14 ms. Code and the full dataset of 390 throws are available (https://tinyurl.com/radardoagit).
