title: TANGO-VIO: Triangulation-Aware Navigation with Guaranteed Feature-Observability for Visual-Inertial Odometry
summary: In vision-aided navigation and visual-inertial odometry, the quality of triangulated three-dimensional feature positions is a fundamental prerequisite for state estimation accuracy. Triangulation becomes ill-conditioned or even impossible when a camera undergoes pure rotation without translation, or when the observed bearing vectors provide insufficient parallax. Even though visual-inertial odometry has been extensively studied, the active maintenance of feature-observability during navigation has not been sufficiently addressed in the literature. To address this gap, this study presents TANGO-VIO, a triangulation-aware navigation framework that embeds a log-determinant metric of the feature-wise stacked-bearing matrix into a control barrier function. In this proposed method, the observability guarantee is established in the feature-geometric sense by enforcing a lower bound on the aggregate triangulation-information metric through a nominal-direction-weighted minimum-deviation velocity correction. The proposed architecture is evaluated through software-inthe- loop simulations and real flight experiments. The results show improved triangulation conditioning under low-parallax motion, while the flight response closely reproduces the corresponding simulation behavior and confirms the practical realizability of the proposed safety filter. Supplementary materials are available on the project webpage.

AI.tldr: TANGO-VIO is a triangulation-aware navigation framework that embeds a log-determinant metric of the stacked-bearing matrix into a control barrier function to maintain feature observability in visual-inertial odometry during low-parallax motion.
AI.motivation: Triangulated 3D feature positions are fundamental for state estimation accuracy in vision-aided navigation and visual-inertial odometry, but triangulation becomes ill-conditioned under pure rotation without translation or insufficient parallax. Active maintenance of feature observability during navigation has been insufficiently addressed in the literature.
AI.method: TANGO-VIO embeds a log-determinant metric of the feature-wise stacked-bearing matrix into a control barrier function. It enforces a lower bound on the aggregate triangulation-information metric through a nominal-direction-weighted minimum-deviation velocity correction, establishing observability guarantees in the feature-geometric sense.
AI.result: Software-in-the-loop simulations and real flight experiments demonstrate improved triangulation conditioning under low-parallax motion, with flight response closely reproducing simulation behavior and confirming practical realizability of the proposed safety filter.
AI.conclusion: The proposed safety filter is practically realizable and effective for maintaining feature observability in navigation scenarios, successfully addressing the gap in active feature-observability maintenance for visual-inertial odometry.

title: Toward Geometry-Scalable Whole-Body Touch for Humanoids: A 3D-Printed Conformal EIT Skin
summary: Whole-body tactile sensing is a prerequisite for humanoids that operate in contact-rich human environments, but conventional taxel arrays scale poorly with surface area, wiring complexity, and robot-specific curvature. We present a conformal electrical impedance tomography tactile skin fabricated through a geometry-adaptable additive-manufacturing workflow. A flexible conductive TPU layer forms a continuous sensing domain, while contact-induced coupling with conductive patches produces boundary voltage changes that are reconstructed using a one-step Gauss-Newton EIT solver. We first characterize the electromechanical design space of the layered structure and show that low-resistance contact-enhancement patches and a porous conductive TPU sensing layer improve sensitivity while preserving printability. We then validate contact localization on a planar prototype, a curved U-shaped prototype, and a qualitative iCub-face-shaped geometry. The curved sensor achieves a mean localization error of 6 mm over 18 contact positions without supervised post-processing. These results suggest that additively manufactured tomographic skins can reduce the morphology-specific redesign burden for humanoid tactile coverage and provide a practical route toward large-area contact sensing for human-centered deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a conformal electrical impedance tomography (EIT) tactile skin fabricated via additive manufacturing, enabling whole-body tactile sensing for humanoids with reduced scaling issues compared to conventional taxel arrays.
AI.motivation: Whole-body tactile sensing is essential for humanoids operating in contact-rich environments, but conventional taxel arrays face limitations in scaling with surface area, wiring complexity, and robot-specific curvature.
AI.method: The researchers developed a geometry-adaptable additive-manufacturing workflow to create a conformal EIT tactile skin featuring a flexible conductive TPU continuous sensing domain and contact-enhancement patches. They implemented a one-step Gauss-Newton EIT solver for reconstruction and characterized the electromechanical design space, validating the system on planar, curved U-shaped, and iCub-face-shaped prototypes.
AI.result: Low-resistance contact-enhancement patches and porous conductive TPU were found to improve sensitivity while preserving printability. The curved sensor achieved a mean localization error of 6 mm across 18 contact positions without supervised post-processing.
AI.conclusion: Additively manufactured tomographic skins can significantly reduce the morphology-specific redesign burden for humanoid tactile coverage and provide a practical pathway toward large-area contact sensing for human-centered deployment.

title: Dynamic UAV-based search operations using probabilistic diffusion modeling of Man Overboard incident victims
summary: More than 70% of the people that fell overboard cruise ships in the period 2010-2019 lost their lives. This paper presents a strategy for reliably predicting the area a person may be in after a man overboard incident, and describes in detail the search methods to find them utilizing UAV technology. The search area prediction method employs an Extended Kalman Filter that capitalizes on the information from the Leeway model to track the missing person in the sea by taking into account the uncertainty of the movement of the person and the weather conditions in the area. Then, a UAV uses this information to search for the person. Five different methods for searching in this dynamic area are presented and evaluated - the Zigzag, the Boustrophedon, the Spiral, the Probability Informed Search and the Improved Probability Informed Search (IPIS) methods. The IPIS method provides success rate of over 80% on average for finding a person, even if the UAV initiates the search mission 20 minutes after the man overboard incident and even assuming a detection method with a success rate of 30%. All code for the simulation environment and the evaluation of the methods is available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/diangeli/pdms-man-overboard.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a comprehensive strategy for searching for missing persons after man overboard incidents on cruise ships. The approach combines an Extended Kalman Filter (tracking the person with Leeway model data) with UAV search operations, evaluating five search methods where the Improved Probability Informed Search (IPIS) achieves over 80% success rate even 20 minutes post-incident.
AI.motivation: Over 70% of people who fell overboard from cruise ships between 2010-2019 died, indicating a critical need for improved search and rescue strategies. Traditional search methods are often inefficient and may fail to locate missing persons quickly, especially in dynamic maritime environments.
AI.method: The method employs an Extended Kalman Filter that incorporates Leeway model data to track the missing person in the sea, accounting for movement uncertainty and weather conditions. A UAV uses this tracking information to search the predicted area. Five search algorithms are evaluated: Zigzag, Boustrophedon, Spiral, Probability Informed Search, and Improved Probability Informed Search (IPIS).
AI.result: The Improved Probability Informed Search (IPIS) method provides an average success rate of over 80% for finding a missing person, even when the UAV initiates the search 20 minutes after the incident and assuming a 30% detection rate for the UAV's sensors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed strategy, particularly the IPIS method, significantly improves the probability of successfully locating missing persons after man overboard incidents. The integration of tracking (Extended Kalman Filter with Leeway model) with intelligent search algorithms enables effective search operations even with delayed response times and imperfect detection capabilities. The open-source code allows for further research and implementation.

title: Look Where It Matters: Adaptive Visual Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Visual representations of VLA models remain unreliable for spatially precise robotic manipulation. We uncover that vision encoders in VLAs also exhibit attention artifacts previously documented in generic Vision Transformers, and further show that, in embodied policies, these artifacts are closely associated with spatial perception capabilities acquired during post-training. As the encoder learns task-relevant information such as object location, depth ordering, and local geometry, limited global-token capacity causes part of this information to spill into low-information patch tokens. We introduce AtVLA, a framework that inserts learnable register tokens into the visual encoder. Trained end-to-end using only embodied data and the original action objective, these registers emerge as dedicated carriers of embodied spatial information, while the remaining patch tokens recover clean and spatially faithful attention distributions crucial for precise target localization and fine-grained contact. Clean attention restores reliable localization, but cannot recover geometric details lost in low-resolution observations. AtVLA therefore couples attention rectification with uncertainty-gated local refinement. The action expert samples multiple action chunks and estimates uncertainty from their disagreement; only for uncertain predictions, action-conditioned attention rollout identifies the task-relevant region, which is cropped, re-encoded at high resolution, and appended to the cached prefix for refined action generation. Across LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and a challenging single-view real-world benchmark, AtVLA improves the average LIBERO success rate from 94.2% to 98.4% and real-world success from 46.5% to 69.0%. The cropping is triggered on approximately 30% of replanning steps, resulting in only 1.4-1.6x the total computation of the base model under the representative deployment setting.

AI.tldr: AtVLA inserts learnable register tokens into vision-language-action model encoders to carry spatial information, coupled with uncertainty-gated local refinement for precise robotic manipulation, improving LIBERO success from 94.2% to 98.4% and real-world success from 46.5% to 69.0% with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Visual representations in VLAs suffer from attention artifacts similar to generic Vision Transformers. These artifacts are associated with spatial perception capabilities acquired during post-training. Limited global-token capacity causes important spatial information to spill into low-information patch tokens, making visual representations unreliable for spatially precise robotic manipulation.
AI.method: AtVLA framework that: (1) inserts learnable register tokens into the visual encoder; (2) trains end-to-end using embodied data and original action objective; (3) registers emerge as dedicated carriers of embodied spatial information; (4) couples attention rectification with uncertainty-gated local refinement; (5) uses action-conditioned attention rollout for uncertain predictions; (6) crops and re-encodes task-relevant regions at high resolution for refined action generation.
AI.result: LIBERO success rate improved from 94.2% to 98.4%; real-world success improved from 46.5% to 69.0%; cropping triggered on ~30% of replanning steps with only 1.4-1.6x total computation overhead of the base model.
AI.conclusion: AtVLA effectively addresses attention artifacts in VLAs through register tokens and uncertainty-gated refinement, significantly improving performance on both simulated (LIBERO, SimplerEnv) and real-world benchmarks while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Clean attention restores reliable localization but cannot recover geometric details lost in low-resolution observations, necessitating the hybrid approach.

title: Learning Panorama-Aware VLA for Mobile Manipulation with Whole-Body Teleoperation
summary: Mobile manipulation is a key capability for embodied intelligence, enabling robots to accomplish complex multi-stage tasks in open-world environments. However, mobile manipulation poses two key challenges for vision-language-action (VLA) policies: At the data level, the efficient collection of high-quality whole-body demonstrations demands the coordinated control of both the mobile base and the robotic arms; at the model level, existing VLA models predominantly rely on local camera observations, whose limited field of view hinders global spatial understanding. To address these challenges, we develop a whole-body teleoperation system and a panoramic-aware VLA policy. The system enables coordinated control of a wheeled bimanual robot through a single VR interface and supports the acquisition of a real-world mobile manipulation dataset comprising 5.5 hours of multimodal demonstrations. Building upon this dataset, we propose PanoVLA, a panorama-aware vision-language-action policy for mobile bimanual manipulation. Built upon a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PanoVLA introduces global spatial context through dedicated panorama encoding and fusion modules, enabling effective integration of panoramic observations with language instructions and robot states for action generation. Evaluation on four real-world mobile manipulation tasks demonstrates that PanoVLA achieves an average stage completion rate of 91.3\% and an end-to-end success rate of 73.4\%, substantially outperforming local-view baselines. These results demonstrate that incorporating panoramic spatial context improves spatial understanding and closed-loop manipulation performance in mobile robots.

AI.tldr: PanoVLA introduces a panoramic-aware vision-language-action policy for mobile bimanual robots that achieves 73.4% end-to-end success rate by integrating panoramic visual context with language instructions and robot states.
AI.motivation: Mobile manipulation for embodied intelligence faces two key challenges: (1) at the data level, efficiently collecting high-quality whole-body demonstrations requires coordinated control of both mobile base and robotic arms; (2) at the model level, existing VLA models predominantly rely on local camera observations with limited field of view, hindering global spatial understanding.
AI.method: The authors developed a whole-body teleoperation system enabling coordinated control of a wheeled bimanual robot through a single VR interface, generating a real-world dataset of 5.5 hours of multimodal demonstrations. Building on this, they proposed PanoVLA, a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that introduces global spatial context through dedicated panorama encoding and fusion modules to effectively integrate panoramic observations with language instructions and robot states for action generation.
AI.result: Evaluation on four real-world mobile manipulation tasks shows PanoVLA achieving an average stage completion rate of 91.3% and an end-to-end success rate of 73.4%, substantially outperforming local-view baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating panoramic spatial context significantly improves spatial understanding and closed-loop manipulation performance in mobile robots, demonstrating the value of global visual awareness for complex mobile manipulation tasks.

title: TS-MAMP: A Remanufactured Agricultural Robot Powered by Second-Life EV Components and NMS-Free On-Device Weed Detection
summary: Agriculture 4.0 robotic systems improve field efficiency yet remain too capital-intensive for the fragmented smallholdings that dominate global agriculture. Meanwhile, a growing number of retired low-speed electric-vehicle (LSEV) powertrains retain functional electromechanical value but are destructively recycled. This paper presents TS-MAMP (Telescopic-Sleeve Modular Agricultural Mobile Platform), a remanufactured robot built under 3R (reduce, reuse, recycle) circular-economy principles. Retired 48 V brushless-DC (BLDC) hub motors are paired via back-EMF matching, and lead-acid battery modules screened at 60%-80% state of health are actively balanced within a 100 mV inter-module voltage deviation. Together, these reused components reduce the powertrain-and-chassis BOM cost by approximately 60%, to below USD 450 (perception and weeding modules excluded). The truss chassis provides >=200 kg static load, continuously adjustable track width from 1200 mm to 2000 mm, and <=5-minute module changeover. An NMS-free (non-maximum-suppression-free) YOLOv10n detector with consistent dual-assignment training and negative-sample learning achieves 80.87% mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 (58.41% mAP@0.5:0.95) on the Wanxi Crop-Weed dataset, and is deployed via FP16 TensorRT on a Jetson Nano, confirming on-device inference feasibility. TS-MAMP demonstrates that retired EV components, under modest screening, can be re-engineered into affordable, AI-enabled agricultural robots--opening a remanufacturing pathway for the smallholder fields that commercial automation leaves unserved.

AI.tldr: TS-MAMP is a remanufactured agricultural mobile robot built from retired electric vehicle components under circular economy principles, achieving ~60% cost reduction and strong AI detection performance.
AI.motivation: Agricultural 4.0 robots are capital-intensive and unsuitable for smallholdings, while retired low-speed electric vehicle powertrains are destructively recycled, representing wasted value.
AI.method: Retired 48V BLDC hub motors paired via back-EMF matching; lead-acid battery modules at 60%-80% state of health actively balanced within 100mV deviation; truss chassis with adjustable track width (1200-2000mm) and ≥200kg static load; ≤5-minute module changeover; NMS-free YOLOv10n detector with dual-assignment training and negative-sample learning; deployed via FP16 TensorRT on Jetson Nano.
AI.result: Powertrain-and-chassis BOM cost reduced by ~60% to below USD 450 (excluding perception and weeding modules); achieved 80.87% mAP@0.5 and 58.41% mAP@0.5:0.95 on Wanxi Crop-Weed dataset; confirmed on-device inference feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Retired EV components, under modest screening, can be re-engineered into affordable, AI-enabled agricultural robots, offering a remanufacturing pathway for smallholder fields that commercial automation leaves unserved.

title: TRACE: Ergodic Trajectory Optimization for Active Scene Reconstruction
summary: Existing active reconstruction systems with Gaussian-splatting maps select observations greedily, optimizing a single next-best-view (NBV) at each step and connecting the chosen views by short-horizon path planning. This greedy decoupling disregards the global structure of scene information, producing inefficient trajectories that waste sensing capacity in transit between selected views. In this work, we study active reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem: the time-averaged spatial statistics of the sensor trajectory should match a target information distribution induced by the current map. Our approach derives this target distribution online from uncertainty and visibility, and calculates ergodic trajectories via a kernel-ergodic horizon planner with gradient flow and footprint depletion, closing the loop between mapping and trajectory optimization. We thoroughly evaluate TRACE on the Replica dataset against the Next-Best-View (NBV) baselines, improving PSNR by 1.5 dB. Code: https://github.com/spikelab-jhu/trace-active-reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TRACE, a novel active reconstruction system for Gaussian-splatting maps that treats reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem rather than greedy NBV selection. It uses kernel-ergodic horizon planning with gradient flow to generate trajectories that achieve time-averaged spatial statistics matching a target information distribution derived from map uncertainty and visibility. TRACE improves PSNR by 1.5 dB over NBV baselines on Replica dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing active reconstruction systems use greedy next-best-view (NBV) selection with short-horizon path planning, which decouples global structure from local optimization. This produces inefficient trajectories that waste sensing capacity during transit between views because it doesn't consider the overall information distribution needed for complete reconstruction.
AI.method: The approach formulates active reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem where the time-averaged spatial statistics of the sensor trajectory should match a target information distribution. The method: 1) Derives this target distribution online from uncertainty and visibility, 2) Calculates ergodic trajectories via a kernel-ergodic horizon planner with gradient flow and footprint depletion, 3) Closes the loop between mapping and trajectory optimization.
AI.result: TRACE is thoroughly evaluated on Replica dataset against Next-Best-View (NBV) baselines, achieving a PSNR improvement of 1.5 dB.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating active reconstruction as an ergodic coverage problem rather than greedy NBV selection, TRACE generates more efficient trajectories that better utilize sensing capacity, leading to improved reconstruction quality (1.5 dB PSNR gain) compared to traditional approaches. The proposed method effectively closes the loop between mapping and trajectory optimization for active reconstruction tasks.

title: Residual-Based Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Legged Robot State Estimation
summary: State estimation is a key component in model-based control of walking robots and, more broadly, applicable wherever hidden variables must be inferred. The Kalman filter is widely used to estimate floating-base position and velocity by fusing multiple sensing modalities. However, tuning noise parameters is challenging and typically requires expert knowledge. Moreover, fixed noise parameters are unsuitable for varying gaits and environments. We propose an online adaptation strategy for the process noise covariance matrix Q and the measurement noise covariance matrix R. Specifically, we introduce a filter residual and innovation-based covariance adaptation method for legged robot state estimation and evaluate it against a baseline approach relying on IMU and foot force measurements. The proposed adaptation is implemented within an Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (InEKF) fusing IMU and leg kinematics. Experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets with a Unitree Go2 quadruped show that adapting R is sufficient and improves accuracy by 25% for the trotting gait compared to the fixed-tuned InEKF. Finally, the proposed residual-based adaptation achieves comparable performance to the foot force approach, without requiring foot force measurements or additional parameter tuning.

AI.tldr: A residual-based covariance adaptation method for Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (InEKF) improves legged robot state estimation by online adaptation of the measurement noise matrix R, achieving 25% accuracy improvement on trotting gait without foot force measurements.
AI.motivation: Kalman filters are widely used for state estimation in walking robots, but tuning process noise (Q) and measurement noise (R) covariance matrices requires expert knowledge and is challenging. Fixed noise parameters are unsuitable for varying gaits and environments, leading to suboptimal estimation performance.
AI.method: An online adaptation strategy for Q and R matrices based on filter residuals and innovations, implemented within an Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (InEKF) fusing IMU and leg kinematics. Evaluated on indoor and outdoor datasets with a Unitree Go2 quadruped, comparing against a baseline approach using IMU and foot force measurements.
AI.result: Adapting R is sufficient; accuracy improved by 25% for the trotting gait compared to the fixed-tuned InEKF. The residual-based adaptation achieves comparable performance to the foot force approach without requiring foot force measurements or additional parameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed residual-based covariance adaptation enables robust, adaptive state estimation for legged robots across different gaits and environments without the need for expert tuning or additional hardware sensors.

title: TravKAN: Fast and Interpretable Nonlinear Traversability Analysis with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Traversability analysis is a fundamental capability for autonomous mobile robots operating in unstructured environments. While modern machine learning approaches such as deep neural networks and gradient-boosted trees achieve strong predictive performance, they lack interpretability and provide limited insight into the underlying terrain-robot interaction dynamics. In this paper, we propose TravKAN, a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-based framework for fast, scalable, and interpretable traversability estimation. TravKAN represents multivariate decision functions through compositions of learnable univariate functions, enabling compact architectures and symbolic extraction of analytic expressions after training. In addition, we introduce a novel set of handcrafted features derived from the reflectivity channel of LiDAR sensors. To the best of our knowledge, reflectivity has not been systematically exploited for handcrafted traversability descriptors, despite its potential to capture material and surface properties complementary to geometric cues. We evaluate TravKAN on public, real-world urban and off-road datasets and compare it against strong baselines. TravKAN achieves strong performance across all metrics, outperforming conventional deep models and approaching the performance of XGBoost. TravKAN-Lite, i.e., TravKAN's symbolic representation, reveals meaningful nonlinear feature interactions and provides a compact, deployment-friendly, and fast analytic model. Ablation studies further show the robustness of our method to architectural variations and quantify the contribution of the proposed reflectivity-based features. These properties make TravKAN attractive for robotic systems requiring transparency, real-time computational efficiency, and interpretability in safety-critical decision-making.

AI.tldr: TravKAN is a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-based framework for fast, scalable, and interpretable traversability estimation using LiDAR reflectivity features, outperforming conventional deep models while providing symbolic representations for deployment-friendly analytic models.
AI.motivation: Modern ML approaches (deep neural networks, gradient-boosted trees) achieve strong predictive performance but lack interpretability and provide limited insight into terrain-robot interaction dynamics, which is problematic for safety-critical robotic applications.
AI.method: TravKAN uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) to represent multivariate decision functions through compositions of learnable univariate functions, enabling compact architectures and symbolic extraction of analytic expressions. It introduces novel handcrafted features derived from LiDAR reflectivity channel to capture material and surface properties complementary to geometric cues.
AI.result: TravKAN achieves strong performance across all metrics on public urban and off-road datasets, outperforming conventional deep models and approaching XGBoost performance. TravKAN-Lite (symbolic representation) reveals meaningful nonlinear feature interactions and provides a compact, deployment-friendly, fast analytic model. Ablation studies demonstrate robustness to architectural variations and quantify the contribution of reflectivity-based features.
AI.conclusion: TravKAN's combination of transparency, real-time computational efficiency, and interpretability makes it attractive for robotic systems requiring safety-critical decision-making capabilities. The method addresses the interpretability gap in modern ML while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

title: ChainVLA: Chaining Vision-Language-Action Queries through a Unified Execution State for Long-Horizon Manipulation
comment: 13 pages (9 main + 4 appendix), 4 figures. Project page: https://muqy1818.github.io/chainvla-web/
summary: Humans perform long-horizon manipulation by retaining knowledge of what earlier actions have established while continuously adapting the motion underway. By contrast, action-chunked vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly replan from the current input at each query. Existing methods preserve either long-term task evidence through memory or short-term motion through action reuse and ensembling, leaving the cross-query handoff incomplete. We introduce ChainVLA, a 1.2B-parameter VLA policy that chains successive queries through a joint and revisable execution state. Progress Context combines a recurrent Working State with sparse event memory to carry observation-derived task progress, while Motion Tail feeds the preceding prediction's unexecuted continuation into state construction and action generation. Together, the two components condition a decoder that regenerates each action horizon under the latest observation, allowing the carried state to guide the next prediction without fixing it. ChainVLA reaches 62.8% average success on RMBench and 98.8% across four LIBERO suites, while removing Motion Tail or Progress Context reduces RMBench success to 11.2% and 3.0%, respectively. These asymmetric ablations are consistent with motion continuity helping preserve the observation stream from which task progress is inferred.

AI.tldr: ChainVLA is a 1.2B-parameter vision-language-action policy that chains successive queries through a joint and revisable execution state using Progress Context (recurrent Working State + sparse event memory) and Motion Tail (prior prediction's unexecuted continuation) to simultaneously preserve long-term task progress and short-term motion continuity, achieving 62.8% average success on RMBench and 98.8% across four LIBERO suites.
AI.motivation: Existing action-chunked VLA policies replan from scratch at each query, creating a disconnect between short-term motion continuity and long-term task progress. Current methods either preserve long-term evidence via memory or short-term motion via action reuse/ensembling, but fail to maintain both simultaneously, limiting performance on long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.method: ChainVLA introduces two key components: 1) Progress Context combines a recurrent Working State with sparse event memory to carry observation-derived task progress across queries, and 2) Motion Tail feeds the preceding prediction's unexecuted continuation into state construction and action generation. Together these condition a decoder that regenerates each action horizon under the latest observation while allowing the carried state to guide predictions without being fixed.
AI.result: ChainVLA achieves 62.8% average success on RMBench and 98.8% across four LIBERO suites. Ablations show Motion Tail and Progress Context are critical: removing Motion Tail reduces RMBench success to 11.2%, while removing Progress Context reduces it to 3.0%, demonstrating the synergistic relationship between motion continuity and task progress inference.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetric ablations confirm that motion continuity helps preserve the observation stream from which task progress is inferred, validating the importance of maintaining both short-term motion and long-term task context simultaneously in long-horizon manipulation policies. ChainVLA demonstrates that chaining queries through a revisable execution state is essential for human-like manipulation performance.

title: StableMimic: Smooth Human-Like Recovery for Humanoid Motion Tracking - Learning Beyond the Tracking Distribution for Structured Post-Fall Behavior
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Preprint, not formally peer-reviewed
summary: Humanoid motion trackers perform reliably within learned tracking distributions, but falls can move the robot into low-height, contact-rich states from which an advancing command is temporarily unreachable. Tracking-only policies may chase infeasible references, producing rapid, large-amplitude limb corrections that increase risk to the robot and its surroundings. We present StableMimic, a unified tracker trained beyond the nominal tracking distribution. Perturbed resets around multiple human get-up references expose prone, supine, off-balance, and intermediate ground-contact states, shaping structured recovery that returns the robot to the trackable region. Because tracking and recovery occupy markedly different state--action distributions, StableMimic uses dedicated experts for each regime and a proprioceptive gate that continuously blends their actions. A hidden successor-state objective teaches human-reference-shaped recovery without exposing reference identity or phase to the deployed Actor; deployment requires no get-up reference, recovery command, trajectory retrieval, or external policy switch. On the complete retargeted LAFAN1 dance subset, StableMimic achieves the lowest errors on all four tracking metrics among five methods. Across 100 matched push-to-fall trials per method, it recovers in 100/100 and attains the lowest values on six of seven post-fall motion and load measures, supporting improved interaction safety under this protocol. Real Unitree G1 dance and standing-reference deployments qualitatively demonstrate bounded limb motion, autonomous recovery, and command resumption.

AI.tldr: StableMimic is a unified humanoid robot tracker that combines tracking and recovery capabilities using specialized experts and a gating mechanism. It achieves superior tracking performance on dance datasets and 100% recovery success rate from falls across 100 trials.
AI.motivation: Humanoid motion trackers are reliable within learned distributions but fail when robots fall into low-height, contact-rich states. Tracking-only policies chase infeasible references, causing rapid, large-amplitude limb corrections that increase risk to robots and their surroundings.
AI.method: StableMimik uses perturbed resets around multiple human get-up references (prone, supine, off-balance, intermediate ground-contact) to shape structured recovery. It employs dedicated experts for tracking and recovery regimes with a proprioceptive gate blending their actions. A hidden successor-state objective teaches recovery without exposing reference identity or phase to the deployed Actor.
AI.result: On LAFAN1 dance subset, StableMimic achieves the lowest errors on all four tracking metrics among five methods. Across 100 matched push-to-fall trials, it recovers in 100/100 cases and attains the lowest values on six of seven post-fall motion and load measures. Real Unitree G1 deployments show bounded limb motion, autonomous recovery, and command resumption.
AI.conclusion: StableMimik provides a unified solution that maintains high tracking performance while enabling safe, autonomous recovery from falls, eliminating the need for external recovery commands, trajectory retrieval, or policy switching during deployment. This significantly improves robot-safety and interaction safety in real-world scenarios.

title: Environmental resilience via morphological diversity within machines
summary: Organisms contain diverse, sensorimotor parts across size scales and rapidly adapt to new environments, while machines contain only inert materials at smaller scales and struggle with surprise. We hypothesize that this agents-within-agents quality of organisms may aid their resilience: increasing experiences with internal physical adversity may pre-train organisms and machines to handle external adversity, such as encounters with new environments. Not only has this hypothesis not yet been articulated, mechanisms enabling this phenomenon have yet to be proposed. Here we show a mechanism by which this can occur: we found that physical connectors, in learning to restore behavior to previously independent, morphologically diverse agents they disrupted by tethering them together, trigger and tame sufficiently diverse disruptions that later encounters with new environments trigger disruptions that fall within this manageable range, enabling the collective to continue behaving properly without any additional learning or adaptation. Further, we found that building collectives from more agents, or more diverse agents, further increases the collective's resilience to new environments. This suggests that not just taming but intentionally creating internal physical adversity may indeed prepare organisms for external adversity, and could do so for machines, if they were built from smaller machines.

AI.tldr: Organisms' "agents-within-agents" structure, which enables them to experience and handle internal physical adversity, may help them better adapt to new environments. Researchers discovered that physical connectors can trigger and tame diverse disruptions, enabling collectives to handle external adversity without additional learning.
AI.motivation: The paper hypothesizes that organisms' ability to rapidly adapt to new environments may be related to their hierarchical structure of sensorimotor parts across size scales, which allows them to experience and handle internal physical adversity. This internal experience may pre-train organisms to better handle external adversity, such as encountering new environments.
AI.method: Researchers tethered morphologically diverse agents together with physical connectors and observed how these connectors helped restore proper behavior. They also tested the effect of building collectives from more agents or more diverse agents.
AI.result: Physical connectors triggered and tamed sufficiently diverse disruptions, enabling collectives to continue behaving properly when encountering new environments without any additional learning or adaptation. Building collectives from more or more diverse agents further increased the collective's resilience to new environments.
AI.conclusion: The researchers concluded that intentionally creating internal physical adversity (e.g., through tethers) can prepare organisms for external adversity, and this principle could apply to machines if they were built from smaller machines.

title: Human-Centered Reflections on Care Robots: A Comparative Study of Caregiver Perspectives
summary: Care robots are increasingly being introduced into healthcare settings, raising important questions about their acceptance and ethical implementation. To better understand these challenges, this study investigates caregivers' perceptions of four categories of care robots: delivering supplies, helping patients into bed, monitoring vital signs, and assisting with mobility. We conducted a mixed-methods study employing a mixed-factorial design in which 298 caregivers from the United States, Mexico, and Chile evaluated all four robot categories. Quantitative measures integrated constructs from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, the Cognitive-Affective-Normative model, and overall acceptance ratings. Qualitative data were collected through open-ended questions and analyzed using a literature-informed ethical framework. The results indicate that participants across countries generally evaluated care robots positively, particularly for logistical and physically demanding tasks rather than those requiring intensive interpersonal interaction. The qualitative findings provide further insight into stakeholders' views of the ethical implications of care robot use. Participants emphasized potential benefits such as reduced workload, lower risk, and greater patient autonomy, while also expressing concerns about dependability, the need for human oversight, and potential job displacement. Although many ethical concerns were shared across countries, participants differed in how they interpreted and prioritized them. These findings advance a context-sensitive and socially informed understanding of responsible design and implementation of care robots.

AI.tldr: This study examined caregivers' perceptions of four categories of care robots (delivering supplies, helping patients into bed, monitoring vital signs, and assisting with mobility) across the United States, Mexico, and Chile using a mixed-methods design. Results show generally positive evaluations, especially for logistical/physical tasks, with shared ethical concerns about dependability and job displacement, but differences in how concerns were prioritized across cultures.
AI.motivation: Care robots are increasingly being introduced into healthcare settings, raising important questions about their acceptance and ethical implementation. This study aims to better understand caregivers' perceptions of care robots to inform responsible design and implementation.
AI.method: Mixed-methods study with a mixed-factorial design. 298 caregivers from the United States, Mexico, and Chile evaluated four robot categories. Quantitative measures integrated constructs from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, the Cognitive-Affective-Normative model, and overall acceptance ratings. Qualitative data collected through open-ended questions and analyzed using a literature-informed ethical framework.
AI.result: Participants across countries generally evaluated care robots positively, particularly for logistical and physically demanding tasks rather than those requiring intensive interpersonal interaction. Qualitative findings highlight potential benefits (reduced workload, lower risk, greater patient autonomy) and concerns (dependability, need for human oversight, potential job displacement). Ethical concerns were shared across countries but participants differed in interpretation and prioritization.
AI.conclusion: These findings advance a context-sensitive and socially informed understanding of responsible design and implementation of care robots, highlighting the importance of considering cultural differences in how ethical concerns are interpreted and prioritized.

title: Certifying Plans under Model Mismatch: A Trilemma for Reachability from Scarce Data
summary: Sim-to-real policies are designed under nominal dynamics, but target-system trials may yield only a few isolated one-step transitions. We study pre-execution certification of a fixed control sequence, such as an action chunk produced by a learned policy. If the sequence reaches an unobserved state-input region, the observations remain consistent with target systems whose trajectories separate along it by an arbitrarily large amount. Any deterministic certifier sound for all of them must then decline to certify or return a reachable tube with arbitrarily large projected width. For bounded smooth classes of the target-nominal model error, we derive a finite plan-dependent projected-width lower bound. These results expose a trilemma among uniform trajectory containment, finite projected width, and unrestricted model-error behavior beyond the observations. ForeReach requires a supplied componentwise Lipschitz bound on the model error. Observed transition pairs can refute this declaration but cannot establish it outside the observed locations. Conditional on a valid declaration, our method constructs a set-membership envelope for the model error, propagates a zonotopic reachable tube, and certifies only when propagation remains within the certification domain and every projected tube slice avoids the unsafe set. In two benchmark systems, calibration baselines may remain narrow after losing trajectory containment outside data support, whereas our method declines to certify unsupported sequences and recovers certification when relevant target data and sufficient obstacle clearance are available.

AI.tldr: ForeReach certifies fixed control sequences for sim-to-real policies by propagating zonotopic reachable tubes under a componentwise Lipschitz bound on model error, providing finite projected-width guarantees that decline certification for unsupported sequences but recover it when relevant target data and obstacle clearance are available.
AI.motivation: Sim-to-real policies are designed under nominal dynamics, but target-system trials yield only a few isolated one-step transitions, creating a need for pre-execution certification of fixed control sequences (action chunks from learned policies).
AI.method: ForeReach requires a supplied componentwise Lipschitz bound on the model error. It constructs a set-membership envelope for the model error, propagates a zonotopic reachable tube, and certifies only when propagation remains within the certification domain and every projected tube slice avoids the unsafe set.
AI.result: For bounded smooth classes of the target-nominal model error, a finite plan-dependent projected-width lower bound is derived. The method exposes a trilemma among uniform trajectory containment, finite projected width, and unrestricted model-error behavior beyond observations.
AI.conclusion: Calibration baselines may remain narrow after losing trajectory containment outside data support. ForeReach declines to certify unsupported sequences but recovers certification when relevant target data and sufficient obstacle clearance are available, demonstrating improved robustness over calibration baselines.

title: Grounded Semantic Re-Binding for Robust Instruction Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in robotic manipulation but suffer catastrophic performance drops when canonical instructions are simply paraphrased. Although this brittleness is typically addressed through costly data scaling, our probing reveals that the root cause is architectural rather than a lack of semantic understanding. Specifically, we demonstrate that current VLAs successfully retain the correct task identity internally. The failure actually stems from the joint encoding of dynamic visual observations and text, which introduces systematic feature shifts. Because the downstream action policy is highly vulnerable to these variations, it fails to translate the preserved semantics into correct control commands. To resolve this structural bottleneck, we propose Grounded Semantic Re-binding (GSR), an elegant intervention that bypasses unstable joint routing by explicitly fusing independently extracted task semantics with native visual features to train a completely re-initialized action expert from scratch. This targeted intervention dramatically restores paraphrastic invariance using only canonical demonstrations. On the LIBERO-Para benchmark, GSR improves success rates by up to 44.6 percent. It enables lightweight models to rival massively scaled baselines and pushes state-of-the-art models to a new record PRIDE score of 70.4, outperforming the recently introduced large-scale pretrained model Xiaomi-Robotics-0 in instruction generation capabilities. Building on these insights, we also introduce ParaVLA, a natively decoupled 0.33B-parameter model exhibiting near-perfect robustness to instruction rewording. Ultimately, our work proves that robust semantic grounding can be achieved through elegant structural design, bypassing the inefficient brute-force data scaling paradigm.

AI.tldr: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models fail when instructions are paraphrased due to architectural issues in joint encoding rather than semantic gaps. The paper proposes Grounded Semantic Re-binding (GSR), which fuses independently extracted task semantics with visual features to train a re-initialized action expert, improving success rates by 44.6% on LIBERO-Para and introducing ParaVLA, a lightweight model with near-perfect paraphrase robustness.
AI.motivation: VLA models suffer catastrophic performance drops when instructions are simply paraphrased. While previous approaches addressed this brittleness through costly data scaling, the authors discovered the root cause is architectural - specifically, the joint encoding of dynamic visual observations and text introduces systematic feature shifts that downstream action policies cannot handle.
AI.method: Grounded Semantic Re-binding (GSR): an intervention that bypasses unstable joint routing by explicitly fusing independently extracted task semantics with native visual features to train a completely re-initialized action expert from scratch using only canonical demonstrations.
AI.result: GSR improves success rates by up to 44.6% on the LIBERO-Para benchmark, enables lightweight models to rival massively scaled baselines, pushes state-of-the-art models to 70.4 PRIDE score (outperforming Xiaomi-Robotics-0), and introduces ParaVLA, a 0.33B-parameter model exhibiting near-perfect robustness to instruction rewording.
AI.conclusion: Robust semantic grounding can be achieved through elegant structural design rather than inefficient brute-force data scaling. The work demonstrates that architectural improvements can dramatically enhance paraphrastic invariance, enabling efficient, lightweight models to match or exceed the performance of massive scaled baselines.

title: Probabilistic Reachable-Action Verification of Visuomotor Policies via Set-Based Training
summary: Reachability analysis for visuomotor policies is difficult because large visual encoders make end-to-end set propagation computationally expensive and excessively conservative. We therefore freeze the visual encoder and confine set propagation to a low-dimensional interface between it and the downstream policy, with the interface set calibrated from held-out camera-pose perturbations. Propagating this set through the policy with zonotopes yields a terminal output-enclosure width that set-based training optimizes directly. During evaluation, camera-pose perturbations are sampled from the prescribed distribution, and rollout-level split conformal calibration converts the resulting action-deviation scores into a probabilistic reachable-action radius with finite-sample coverage. In controlled manipulation experiments, set-based training reduces this radius while preserving closed-loop task capability, and matched behavior-only, observational-consistency, and pointwise-adversarial controls all leave a larger radius.

AI.tldr: Reachability analysis for visuomotor policies is challenging due to large visual encoders making end-to-end set propagation computationally expensive and overly conservative. The authors freeze the visual encoder and confine set propagation to a low-dimensional interface, using zonotopes for propagation and split conformal calibration to estimate a probabilistic reachable-action radius with finite-sample coverage.
AI.motivation: Large visual encoders make end-to-end set propagation for visuomotor policies computationally expensive and overly conservative, making reachability analysis difficult.
AI.method: Freeze visual encoder; confine set propagation to low-dimensional interface calibrated from camera-pose perturbations; use zonotopes for propagation; terminal output-enclosure width optimized via set-based training; evaluate using rollout-level split conformal calibration to convert action-deviation scores into probabilistic reachable-action radius.
AI.result: Set-based training reduces the reachable-action radius while preserving closed-loop task capability. Compared to behavior-only, observational-consistency, and pointwise-adversarial controls, the proposed method achieves a significantly smaller radius.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables tighter reachability bounds for visuomotor policies while maintaining task performance, outperforming alternative control methods in terms of providing more precise probabilistic reachable-action radius estimates.

title: Why Does Action Chunking Improve Behavioral Cloning Performance in Robotic Control?
summary: Action chunking---predicting and executing multiple actions instead of a single action---has proven to be a critical component for learning effective robotic control policies. However, our precise understanding of why action chunking improves performance has remained limited. In this work we seek to close this gap. Through rigorous experimental evaluations in both simulated and real-world settings, we show that existing hypotheses for the success of action chunking---temporal consistency, horizon reduction, and representation learning---fail to explain the success of action chunking. Instead, we find that action chunking benefits from greater non-Markovian expressivity and reduced compounding error compared to Markovian policies, but, in many settings of interest, these effects can be fully captured by delayed policies, which at each step predict a single action based on the observation $k$ steps in the past. We then show that there exists an additional benefit of action chunking that we refer to as implicit ensembling. In particular, by learning a diversity of temporal relationships (that is, $a_t | o_t, a_t | o_{t-1}, \ldots$), action-chunked policies exhibit behavior matching that of a model ensemble, increasing their robustness and generalization ability over policies that only learn a single temporal relationship. Building on these insights, we show that in simulated and real-world robotic control settings, we can match the performance of action chunking without action chunking---by deploying an action chunking policy as an ensemble of policies with randomized delays. Furthermore, we propose a policy class that amplifies the benefits of action chunking by explicitly instantiating an ensemble, and which we show significantly improves over the performance of action chunking in many domains.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why action chunking improves robotic control performance. It shows that existing explanations (temporal consistency, horizon reduction, representation learning) are insufficient. Instead, action chunking benefits from greater non-Markovian expressivity, reduced compounding error, and implicit ensembling. The authors demonstrate that action chunking can be replaced by ensembles of delayed policies, and propose an explicit ensemble policy class that outperforms standard action chunking.
AI.motivation: While action chunking (predicting/executing multiple actions instead of a single action) has proven effective in robotic control, there has been limited understanding of why it works. Existing hypotheses include temporal consistency, horizon reduction, and representation learning, but these fail to fully explain the success of action chunking.
AI.method: The authors conducted rigorous experimental evaluations in both simulated and real-world robotic control settings. They examined existing hypotheses and tested the benefits of action chunking versus delayed policies. They also proposed a policy class that explicitly instantiates an ensemble to amplify action chunking benefits.
AI.result: Existing hypotheses fail to explain action chunking's success. Action chunking benefits from greater non-Markovian expressivity and reduced compounding error, which can be captured by delayed policies. Additionally, action chunking provides implicit ensembling benefits through learning diverse temporal relationships. The authors showed that action chunking can be matched by ensembles of delayed policies, and their proposed explicit ensemble policy class significantly outperforms standard action chunking.
AI.conclusion: Action chunking's effectiveness stems from implicit ensembling (learning diverse temporal relationships) beyond non-Markovian expressivity and reduced compounding error. These benefits can be achieved through ensembles of delayed policies, and explicit ensemble instantiation further improves performance, providing a practical alternative to standard action chunking in robotic control.

title: Situation Aware Frontier Prioritization for Quadruped Search and Rescue
summary: Quadruped robots are a promising platform for search and rescue missions because they can navigate cluttered indoor environments that may be restrictive for wheeled systems. However, in unknown rescue scenarios, autonomous exploration must balance map expansion with the likelihood of finding victims, which is not explicitly addressed by clas- sical frontier selection strategies. This paper presents a situation aware frontier prioritization method for single robot quadruped search and rescue. The proposed approach preserves the frontier exploration framework, but extends frontier ranking with information gain, observation deficit, rescue relevance, terrain penalty, and travel cost. The method is eval- uated in Gazebo simulation with a quadruped robot in two indoor rescue scenarios with different levels of difficulty. The first scenario is used as a sanity check, while the second introduces stronger clutter and frontier ambiguity. Experimental results show that all methods perform reliably in a simple scenario, whereas in a complex scenario is different. In that setting, the proposed method achieves the highest completion rate and the highest victim recovery among the evaluated approaches. These results indicate that situation aware frontier prioritization is beneficial when frontier choice becomes nontrivial and rescue utility must be balanced against generic exploration objectives.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a situation-aware frontier prioritization method for quadruped robots in search and rescue missions, extending frontier exploration with information gain, observation deficit, rescue relevance, terrain penalty, and travel cost to better balance map expansion with victim finding.
AI.motivation: Quadruped robots are promising for search and rescue but classical frontier selection strategies don't explicitly address the balance between map expansion and finding victims in unknown rescue scenarios.
AI.method: The approach preserves the frontier exploration framework but extends frontier ranking with five factors: information gain, observation deficit, rescue relevance, terrain penalty, and travel cost.
AI.result: Evaluated in Gazebo simulation with a quadruped robot in two indoor rescue scenarios. In a simple scenario, all methods performed reliably. In a complex scenario with stronger clutter and frontier ambiguity, the proposed method achieved the highest completion rate and highest victim recovery.
AI.conclusion: Situation-aware frontier prioritization is beneficial when frontier choice becomes nontrivial and rescue utility must be balanced against generic exploration objectives.

title: CoWAM: Coordination Contracts for Selective Policy Intervention with WAMs
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) augment robot policies with action-conditioned predicted futures, but a plausible future alone does not justify changing the action that a bimanual policy would execute. We present CoWAM, a selective intervention layer that expresses synchronization, role compatibility, and collision convergence as coordination contracts. Each contract combines typed admissibility checks with event-conditioned verification and calibrated intervention gates. CoWAM preserves the nominal action unless an alternative satisfies every active obligation and provides a clear, low-risk improvement; when the nominal action is also inadmissible, it invokes a predefined abstention fallback. To separate selector quality from proposal quality, all methods operate on identical candidate pools and commit their decisions before shared oracle labeling. Across eight simulated bimanual tasks, CoWAM improves coordination-valid selection by 16.7 percentage points over the contract-only variant and raises closed-loop success by 9.6 percentage points over the strongest selective baseline, while keeping harmful interventions below 1%. Together, these results establish coordination contracts as an effective interface for conservative policy intervention with predicted world-action evidence across coordination-rich bimanual tasks.

AI.tldr: CoWAM introduces a selective intervention layer that uses coordination contracts to improve bimanual robot policy coordination by selecting better actions while maintaining safety.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) predict action-conditioned futures, but having a plausible future alone does not justify changing the robot's action. There is a need for a mechanism to selectively intervene only when it makes sense.
AI.method: CoWAM expresses synchronization, role compatibility, and collision convergence as coordination contracts. Each contract combines typed admissibility checks, event-conditioned verification, and calibrated intervention gates. The approach preserves the nominal action unless an alternative satisfies all active obligations with clear improvement; when the nominal action is inadmissible, it uses a predefined abstention fallback.
AI.result: Across eight simulated bimanual tasks: (1) CoWAM improves coordination-valid selection by 16.7 percentage points over contract-only variant, (2) raises closed-loop success by 9.6 percentage points over strongest selective baseline, (3) keeps harmful interventions below 1%.
AI.conclusion: Coordination contracts establish an effective interface for conservative policy intervention with predicted world-action evidence across coordination-rich bimanual tasks.

title: Ego2Robot: Scalable Robot Data Synthesis from Egocentric Human Data
summary: Learning generalizable robot manipulation policies requires large-scale and diverse demonstration data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer rich scene and task diversity, and prior work has shown that retargeting and rendering such videos into robot-format data can yield effective per-task policies at small scale. However, whether this approach can provide pretraining benefits for vision-language-action models at scale remains unexplored. We present \textbf{Ego2Robot}, a scalable pipeline that converts egocentric human manipulation videos into robot training data through action retargeting, robot-arm visual synthesis, and multi-level quality curation. Ego2Robot supports both curated datasets and in-the-wild videos, producing 18,561 hours of robot training data spanning 15 robot morphologies, making it the largest ego-to-robot dataset to date. To evaluate generalization, we extend RoboTwin2.0 with disentangled perturbation axes covering visual appearance, scene layout, embodiment morphology, and task semantics. Experiments show that joint pretraining on Ego2Robot-synthesized and robot data consistently improves out-of-distribution generalization across multiple perturbation types, with benefits validated on real-robot deployment. Project page: https://www-ye.github.io/ego2robot_blog/

AI.tldr: Ego2Robot is a scalable pipeline that converts egocentric human manipulation videos into robot training data (18,561 hours spanning 15 robot morphologies) via action retargeting, robot-arm visual synthesis, and multi-level quality curation, demonstrating that joint pretraining with this synthetic data significantly improves out-of-distribution generalization for vision-language-action models in robot manipulation.
AI.motivation: Learning generalizable robot manipulation policies requires large-scale and diverse demonstration data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer rich scene and task diversity, but prior work has not explored whether this approach can provide pretraining benefits for vision-language-action models at scale.
AI.method: Ego2Robot pipeline with three key components: (1) action retargeting to map human actions to robot trajectories, (2) robot-arm visual synthesis to generate robot-centric viewpoints, and (3) multi-level quality curation. The system supports both curated datasets and in-the-wild videos.
AI.result: Produces 18,561 hours of robot training data spanning 15 robot morphologies, the largest ego-to-robot dataset to date. Joint pretraining on Ego2Robot-synthesized and robot data consistently improves out-of-distribution generalization across perturbation types (visual appearance, scene layout, embodiment morphology, task semantics), with benefits validated on real-robot deployment.
AI.conclusion: Converting egocentric human manipulation videos into robot training data through Ego2Robot effectively pretrains vision-language-action models and significantly enhances their generalization capabilities across diverse perturbations, validating the approach for scalable robot manipulation policy learning.
